The sizes of EUC and SUC vary with the twist angle 
 and periodicity 
 (Fig. 2g, h). Furthermore, in square lattices, the EUC size diverges near high-symmetry directions (e.g., 45°), reflecting discrete commensurate matching conditions. This divergence is a hallmark of moiré lattices42, underscoring their extreme sensitivity to angular alignment and the discrete symmetries of the host lattice. Both the divergence of the EUC and the discrete growth of the SUC originate from the intrinsic incompatibility between continuous geometric parameters and discrete integer commensurability, which forces increasingly large integer solutions near incommensurate conditions, a fundamental mechanism underlying moiré physics.

Likewise, the SUC size exhibits a complex dependence on the perturbation period (Fig. 2h), with discrete jumps corresponding to different rational commensurability ratios. The plotted configurations represent solutions to the two Diophantine equations, with integer parameters constrained to 
. Such sensitivity necessitates the careful selection of rational commensurate conditions that ensure manageable EUC and SUC sizes for computational feasibility. Note that while a square lattice is used as the host lattice example here, the proposed framework is equally applicable to other types of Bravais lattices (Supplementary Note 1).

Momentum-resolved analysis of momentum-encoded metasurfaces
In this section, we apply the directional moiré superlattice framework to metasurfaces in which the surface phase is spatially encoded on each meta-atom to control radiation channels. As illustrated in Fig. 3a, phase encoding can be implemented by introducing geometric perturbations across a square-lattice metasurface. Here, we primarily consider cylindrical meta-atoms for clarity; however, the framework is not limited to meta-atom shape and remains applicable to any scatterer geometry, including anisotropic meta-atoms that rely on rotational perturbations to produce Pancharatnam–Berry (PB) geometric phase22,43; this generality is further supported by full-wave simulations and experimental measurements on PB-type momentum-encoded metasurfaces (Supplementary Note 2).

Fig. 3: Momentum-resolved analysis of directional moiré superlattices.
Fig. 3: Momentum-resolved analysis of directional moiré superlattices.
Full size image
a Conceptual illustration of a directional moiré superlattice formed by applying a one-dimensional periodic perturbation (periodicity λp) onto a two-dimensional host lattice, resulting in a compact SUC. b Schematic depiction of diffraction orders generated by the momentum-encoded metasurface under illumination. Target, aliasing, and stray diffraction orders are indicated. c Discretized radiation channels in reciprocal space, classifying diffraction into target, zeroth-order, aliasing, and stray orders. d Momentum-resolved diffraction efficiency maps showing how target-order diffraction performance varies with meta-atom refractive index. Each momentum-space point represents a target diffraction order defined by the directional moiré superlattice, and the color indicates the corresponding diffraction efficiency. e Influence of lattice periodicity (from 300 to 450 nm) on the emergence and evolution of aliasing diffraction orders. The dotted lines denote the sampling criterion obtained from multi-dimensional sampling theory.

When engineering the far-field response, the design generally follows the principles of the generalized Snell’s law14, in which phase gradients are introduced to redirect light toward a target direction. Once the phase-encoded directional moiré metasurface is constructed, the resulting radiative channels include the zeroth-order non-diffracted beam, the target diffraction order, the aliasing orders that emerge when the spatial sampling condition is not satisfied1,2, and stray orders caused by unwanted near-field coupling and fabrication imperfections. Except for the target order, all remaining diffraction components can be interpreted as undesired diffractions.

As discussed in the previous section, when the encoded momentum and host lattice satisfy both angular alignment and length commensurability, a superlattice can be constructed, allowing us to define a SUC with a well-defined 2D periodicity. This periodicity induces a discretized momentum basis, such that each radiative channel corresponds to a distinct diffraction order, enabling a physically intuitive classification of all scattered directions (Fig. 3c). The reciprocal lattice vectors of SUC are defined as

 and 
 is the integer scaling factor introduced by the second commensurability condition. In the far-field scattering process, all momentum transfers

 in the reciprocal momentum basis of SUC. If the spatial sampling condition is violated due to coarse meta-atom spacing, additional aliasing components appear, described by

 and 
 are the reciprocal lattice vectors of the host lattice, since the host lattice acts as a sampling lattice, where the encoded spectrum in the Fourier space of the metasurface is replicated at intervals of

. We further define stray orders as diffraction orders that do not fall into the target or aliasing directions.

Through this order classification of discretized far-field components, it becomes possible to benchmark metasurfaces in a momentum-resolved manner, even for aperiodic or nonuniform phase profiles. Figure 3d, e show calculated diffraction orders—including target and aliasing components—for each encoded momentum, assuming cylindrical meta-atoms with a full 2π phase coverage and known refractive index and lattice parameters. In these momentum-space maps, each point corresponds to a diffraction order defined by the directional moiré superlattice, while the color scale represents the calculated diffraction efficiency coupled into that order. We note that, unlike PB-type meta-atoms whose phase varies linearly with rotation angle, the phase response of cylindrical meta-atoms does not follow a linear dependence on diameter; therefore, all encoded perturbations were implemented using precomputed nonlinear diameter–phase lookup tables rather than assuming linear scaling (look-up tables are in Supplementary Note 3). In Fig. 3d, as the refractive index of the meta-atoms decreases, diffraction efficiency tends to drop. This occurs because low-index meta-atoms are unable to sufficiently confine incident light, leading to enhanced interactions between adjacent meta-atoms44 and, consequently, a breakdown of the periodic approximation34,35 commonly assumed in meta-atom design. Since most phase maps are extracted under periodic assumptions, performance degradation becomes more severe for higher momentum encodings and lower refractive indices. The supercell-based simulation framework successfully captures these effects, offering a physically realistic assessment of diffraction performance.

Interestingly, the behavior of aliasing orders further illustrates the predictive power of this framework. In Fig. 3e, we calculate the coupling efficiency of aliasing orders for varying lattice periods under different encoded momenta. The dashed boundaries in each graph are analytically derived from multi-dimensional sampling theory1,2 and correspond to the onset of aliasing. The simulation results conform precisely to these theoretical boundaries, validating the accuracy of the momentum-resolved analysis. As the lattice period increases, higher-order components in the spatial frequency spectrum are more readily coupled out, and the aliasing behavior exhibits a strong dependence on the direction of the encoded momentum. This directional dependence highlights the need for a fully momentum-resolved, multi-dimensional treatment of sampling in metasurface design. To our knowledge, this presents the first comprehensive calculation of sampling performance in metasurfaces that is fully resolved in momentum space. Without leveraging the supercell framework, evaluating each momentum encoding would require full-wave simulations of finite-sized metasurfaces—an approach that is computationally demanding and less generalizable.

Directional moiré superlattices in non-local metasurfaces
In the previous section, we focused on the role of the lattice as a local regime, i.e., sampling lattice, and analyzed its behavior within the moiré superlattice framework. In this section, we extend our discussion to demonstrate that the same geometric framework remains valid even when the lattice operates both locally and non-locally in tandem. Notably, recent work33 has demonstrated that introducing the gradient of Berry phase in a non-local metasurface (or photonic crystal slab) can shift Dirac cones at high symmetric points in the Brillouin zone into the light cone, enabling efficient coupling of guided modes to free-space radiation. Here, the moiré superlattice framework can systematically describe and control the directional moiré patterns arising from Berry-phase-encoded photonic crystals.

We consider a hole-based honeycomb photonic crystal (Fig. 4a). This structure features a lattice constant of 260 nm and a complex refractive index of n = 2 + 0.005i, with the imaginary part introduced to account for optical losses in the calculation. The lattice comprises two distinct sublattices: anisotropic elliptical holes (sublattice A, minor and major axes of 58 and 98 nm, respectively) and isotropic circular holes (sublattice B, diameter of 120 nm). This structural asymmetry breaks the inversion symmetry between the two sublattices, thereby opening Dirac gaps at the K and K′ points of the Brillouin zone (Fig. 4a, b). Throughout this work, we use the term “Dirac cone” to refer to these gapped valley dispersions at K and K′, following the convention widely adopted in the valley photonics literature.

Fig. 4: Demonstration of valley addressability by directional moiré metasurfaces.
Fig. 4: Demonstration of valley addressability by directional moiré metasurfaces.
Full size image
a Real-space design flow: starting from a C6-symmetric honeycomb lattice, inversion-symmetry breaking reduces the symmetry to C3 and defines inequivalent sublattices A and B, opening a gap at the Dirac point. A 1D Berry-phase gradient with wavevector kp is then encoded selectively on sublattice A, forming a directional moiré superlattice supercell composed of multiple EUCs. b Momentum-space picture: inversion-symmetry breaking gaps the Dirac cones at K and K′, while the subsequent Berry-phase encoding imparts opposite momentum shifts, +kp and −kp, to the valley states. This displacement folds the valley dispersions into the light cone, enabling radiative coupling and valley-selective addressing. c Distribution of kp vectors satisfying the directional moiré superlattice condition. d SUCs corresponding to the four superlattice configurations marked in (c). e Calculated angle-resolved CD distributions at f = 520 THz for the SUCs shown in (d). Blue and red contours indicate opposite CD signs, originating from spin-valley selective coupling of the Dirac cones at K and K′. Each encoded Rashba momentum is illustrated in the Brillouin zone.

Then, applying an in-plane rotational perturbation to sublattice A introduces spin-dependent momentum shifts, analogous to the Rashba effect31,32,33 (Fig. 4a, b). Consequently, the Dirac cones located at the K and K′ valleys undergo momentum displacements, which move them from outside to inside the light cone at the target frequency. Specifically, the Dirac cone at K shifts by +
, while its time-symmetry conjugate at K’ shifts by −
 (Fig. 4b).

We next identify perturbation momenta 
, that satisfy the angular and length commensurability conditions required for superlattice formation. Figure 4c presents candidate perturbation momentum vectors for encoding, represented as the post-encoding positions of the Dirac cone at the K point. From these, we select four representative vectors (highlighted by red rectangles in Fig. 4c) that ensure the Dirac cones lie within the light cone (shown as a dotted circle) while also limiting the SUC size to a manageable computational scale, defined as det(
) < 30. Note that these vectors are selected for demonstrative purposes. Figure 4d illustrates the resulting SUCs, each annotated with their respective commensurability indices [m1, m2; p, q].

To confirm the directional relocation of Dirac cones into the light cone, we perform angle-resolved simulations under periodic boundary conditions at a frequency of 520 THz using circularly polarized light. We adopt the rigorous coupled-wave analysis for simulation. Figure 4e presents the resulting circular dichroism (CD) distributions, defined as the absorption difference between right- and left-circularly polarized incident light. These reveal Dirac cone cross-sections shifted into the light cone according to the encoded perturbation momenta. Owing to intrinsic spin-valley locking at the K and K′ valleys, each shifted Dirac cone exhibits distinct valley-selective circular polarization, which appears as red or blue contours corresponding to opposite CD signs. The calculated band structures for each photonic crystal slab are in Supplementary Note 4.

Having established the superlattice conditions and the predicted momentum-space relocation of the valley modes, we next experimentally test whether these commensurability-defined shifts can be directly observed. To experimentally validate the proposed directional moiré superlattice framework in the context of valley addressing, we fabricate momentum-encoded photonic crystal slabs using a silicon nitride (Si₃N₄) thin film with a thickness of 70 nm. The structures are defined by electron-beam lithography to create a resist mask, followed by dry etching to transfer the designed patterns into the Si₃N₄ layer. (see “Methods” section) The fabricated lattice consists of a hexagonal arrangement with a period of 310 nm. The anisotropic sublattice A is composed of elliptical holes with major and minor axes of 130 and 65 nm, respectively, while sublattice B consists of circular holes with a diameter of 140 nm. Due to fabrication constraints, the geometric parameters of the fabricated samples are slightly modified from those used in the numerical calculations in Fig. 4. In particular, the lattice period and feature sizes are adjusted to ensure reliable pattern transfer and structural fidelity. Nevertheless, these modifications do not affect the essential physics governed by geometric commensurability.

To probe the momentum-resolved photonic response, angle-resolved measurements are performed along a 1D trajectory in momentum space (Fig. 5). Since the valley modes originate from Dirac cones that are selectively shifted into the light cone along specific directions, it is necessary to align the measurement axis with the encoded momentum direction. To achieve this, each sample is physically rotated such that the momentum-shift direction of the valley modes coincides with the fixed scanning axis of the measurement system. This alignment enables direct access to the relevant band dispersion within the measurable angular range, effectively capturing the photonic band structure along a 1D momentum cut intersecting the shifted valleys.

Fig. 5: Experimental validation of valley addressing enabled by directional moiré superlattices.
Fig. 5: Experimental validation of valley addressing enabled by directional moiré superlattices.
Full size image
a–d SEM images of fabricated momentum-encoded photonic crystal slabs with different orientations of the encoded momentum relative to the underlying lattice. The white rectangles indicate the corresponding superlattice unit cells defined by the commensurability conditions. Scale bars, 500 nm. e–h Corresponding momentum-space representations of each configuration. The hexagonal Brillouin zone of the host lattice is shown with high-symmetry points K and K′. The dashed circle denotes the light cone, within which radiative channels can be accessed. Bottom panels, angle-resolved circular dichroism (CD) measurements as a function of incident angle and wavelength. Distinct CD features corresponding to momentum-shifted valley modes are observed and systematically evolve with the encoded momentum direction, consistent with the predicted relocation of the valley states in momentum space.

As shown in Fig. 5, the angle-resolved CD measurements reveal distinct spectral features that systematically evolve with the orientation of the encoded momentum. Here, CD is defined as the transmission difference between right- and left-circularly polarized incident light. These features correspond to the momentum-shifted valley modes predicted by the directional moiré superlattice analysis. The observed agreement between the measured CD response and the theoretical momentum-space picture confirms that the proposed framework accurately captures the redistribution of radiative channels and enables deterministic valley addressing in momentum-encoded photonic crystal slabs.

Discussion
We have introduced a geometric framework that identifies hidden periodicity in momentum-encoded metasurfaces and represents otherwise aperiodic structures as fully periodic superlattices through a two-step commensurability process. The key strength of this framework lies in its generality. While our demonstration focused on linear phase perturbations derived from the generalized Snell’s law14, the underlying formulation is not limited to such cases. Arbitrary periodic perturbations—including nonlinear, non-analytic, or superposed functions—can be incorporated, as long as the commensurability conditions are satisfied (Supplementary Note 5). Moreover, the methodology is inherently modality-agnostic: relying solely on geometric symmetry and lattice matching, it is readily applicable to various wave-based systems, such as electronics, acoustics, and mechanical metamaterials. Moreover, the lattice does not have to be a discrete system; our formulation accommodates a spatially continuous potential lattice38. Beyond single-directional perturbations, our framework naturally extends to bi-directional configurations (Supplementary Note 6). Beyond far-field radiation and coupling-process engineering demonstrated in this work, the directional moiré superlattice framework may, in principle, be extended to explore other lattice-driven phenomena governed by commensurability and symmetry. For example, moiré-induced flat-band physics37,38,39,40, widely studied in electronic and photonic systems, naturally arises from long-period supercell formation. While such phenomena are beyond the scope of the present study, our framework provides a compact and deterministic geometric basis that could facilitate their systematic investigation in momentum-encoded metasurfaces.

Nonetheless, several limitations remain. Notably, our current formulation assumes a uniform momentum encoding across the metasurface. In practical scenarios, e.g., metalenses3,5,6, the phase gradient varies continuously across space, locally spanning a spectrum of momenta. Under such conditions, the concept of a single supercell breaks down, and the advantages of periodic simplification are diminished. However, even in these cases, the directional moiré framework offers value as a momentum-resolved benchmarking tool without relying on the local periodic approximations34,35. By evaluating metasurface responses under individual momentum encodings, one can indirectly assess the performance of a meta-atom library, providing physical insights into the bandwidth, sampling fidelity, and diffraction efficiency. Finally, the directional moiré framework presents a fundamentally distinct design paradigm compared to traditional bilayer moiré systems36,37,38,39,40,41, which rely solely on global twist angles between lattices. By introducing two independent commensurability conditions—angular alignment and length matching—our framework offers greater geometric flexibility and design freedom. This dual-commensurate approach expands the accessible design space for realizing programmable supercell physics.

Fabrication of directional moiré metasurfaces
Metasurfaces were fabricated on a glass substrate with a 500 μm thickness. As a first step, a 70 nm-thick layer of silicon nitride (Si3N4) was deposited using plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD, BMR Technology HiDep-SC). A layer of positive tone photoresist (ZEP 520 A) was spin-coated at 5000 rpm onto the Si3N4 film and subsequently baked at 180 °C for 2 min. High-speed electron-beam lithography (ELS-BODEN, Ellionoix) was used to transfer the metasurface patterns onto the photoresist. The exposed photoresist patterns were developed by immersing the sample in ZEP developer (ZED-N50) at 0 °C for 1 min. The ZEP patterns were transferred onto the silicon nitride film using a dry etching process (DRM85DD, TEL). Finally, the remaining ZEP was removed by immersing it in the anisole solvent.

Could Columbus become a quantum technology hub? Inside Ohio State’s work
Story by Amani Bayo, Columbus Dispatch • 21h • 2 min read


The Columbus Dispatch
Ezekiel Johnston-Halperin on quantum physics and Columbus’ technological future
The Dispatch presents Columbus in Color,
Current Time 
0:00
/
Duration 
1:07:41
0
A quantum computer powerful enough to break much of today’s digital encryption may still be years away, but the race to prepare for that future is already underway.

And some of that work is happening in Columbus.

"If we can get the quantum networking going, there’s a bit of an arms race," Ohio State University physics professor Ezekiel Johnston-Halperin said on the latest episode of Columbus in Color.

Online Courses For Adults
Online Courses For Adults
University of Phoenix
·
Sponsored
call to action icon
Johnston-Halperin is a co-director of Ohio State’s Center for Quantum Information Science and Engineering and leads an Ohio State team participating in the National Science Foundation’s National Quantum Virtual Laboratory program.

Backed by a $4 million planning grant, the team is developing a quantum sensing testbed designed to bring university researchers, national laboratories and industry partners together. The initial grant covers two years of planning for a potential five- to six-year project receiving up to $50 million.

“We want to serve the public good with the work that we’re doing,” Johnston-Halperin said.

What could quantum technology be used for?
Quantum physics describes the behavior of atoms and other particles that form the building blocks of nature. While the subject can sound abstract, Johnston-Halperin said it already underlies much of modern life, including medicine, smartphones, solar panels and other technologies.

Your Boss Will Hate These Games, But You’ll Love Them!
Your Boss Will Hate These Games, But You’ll Love Them!
top5onlinegames.com
top5onlinegames.com
·
Sponsored
call to action icon
Ohio State’s project focuses on quantum sensing, which uses the properties of atoms to measure the world with extreme precision. Researchers are exploring how the sensors could eventually detect radiation, support nuclear and fusion energy or help scientists study molecules and structures within cells.

The challenge now is determining where quantum sensors can solve problems that existing technology cannot.

“We know we can build a quantum sensor,” Johnston-Halperin said. “What’s it good for?”

Answering that question requires physicists and engineers to work alongside specialists in fields such as biology and medicine. Ohio State is also developing graduate programs that cross traditional academic boundaries, combining areas including physics, chemistry, mathematics, computer science and engineering.


Ezekiel Johnston-Halperin is a professor of physics at The Ohio State University whose research focuses on quantum sensing and secure communications. He is helping lead a $4 million National Science Foundation project aimed at advancing quantum technology while strengthening Columbus’ place in the growing field.
Ezekiel Johnston-Halperin is a professor of physics at The Ohio State University whose research focuses on quantum sensing and secure communications. He is helping lead a $4 million National Science Foundation project aimed at advancing quantum technology while strengthening Columbus’ place in the growing field.
© Patrick Flaherty/Columbus Dispatch
Could Columbus become a quantum technology hub?
Johnston-Halperin believes Columbus and the Midwest have the ingredients to become major players in the emerging industry.

He pointed to the region’s research universities, manufacturing history and existing technology infrastructure. One of the earliest connections in ARPANET, a precursor to the modern internet, linked computing systems in Columbus and Chicago.

Tirzepatide: The GLP1 That Crushes It
Tirzepatide: The GLP1 That Crushes It
Direct Meds GLP-1
Direct Meds GLP-1
·
Sponsored
call to action icon
Ohio State is also supporting a second quantum testbed led by the University of Michigan and collaborating with researchers in Illinois.

"There really is sort of a Midwestern moment happening," Johnston-Halperin said.

For him, that work reflects Ohio State’s responsibility as a land-grant university to serve people across the state. It also offers Columbus another opportunity to build on the growth it has experienced over the past decade.

"I think Columbus has been having a moment," he said. "And I see a trajectory for that moment to continue."

Trending reporter Amani Bayo can be reached at abayo@dispatch.com.

The 9 hidden patterns scientists are just beginning to notice
Story by Jeff Blaumberg • 4mo
A Third Type of Magnetism Hiding in Plain Sight
©The author is owner, CC BY-SA 2.0 br
Until recently, physics recognized only two types of magnetism: ferromagnetism, where all magnetic moments align in the same direction - the force that makes refrigerator magnets stick - and antiferromagnetism, where moments align in a regular pattern but point in opposite directions, canceling each other out externally. For generations, that was considered the complete picture. It wasn't.

Altermagnetism was first theorized in 2019 and experimentally confirmed in 2024 by researchers at Mainz University. It bridges the gap between traditional magnetic classifications, offering practical applications in advanced data storage systems. The findings could lead to the development of new magnetic memory devices with the potential to increase operation speeds of up to a thousand times.

What makes the discovery stranger is how ordinary the materials involved turned out to be: there are at least 200 different materials currently known to exhibit altermagnetism.

Does law make lending someone your car a federal offense starting in November?
Story by Laerke Christensen • 1mo • 4 min read


A white person wearing a blue sweater drops a set of car keys into the hand of a white person wearing a grey top. Getty Images, accessed via Canva
A white person wearing a blue sweater drops a set of car keys into the hand of a white person wearing a grey top. Getty Images, accessed via Canva

Claim:

From Nov. 22, lending your vehicle to a person who is not the registered owner will be a federal offense resulting in a $1000 fine.

Rating:

False (About this rating?)

In July 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that, starting Nov. 22, lending a vehicle to anyone other than the registered owner would be a federal offense resulting in a $1,000 fine.

For example, one Facebook page shared the claim on July 23, 2026. The page's post featured a video with a robotic voice that said: 

Starting November 22, lending your vehicle to anyone will officially be considered a federal offense. The new regulation goes into effect without exceptions and only the person registered on the vehicle's documentation will be legally allowed to drive it. The penalty is immediate — a $1,000 fine on the spot with no warnings, no grace period and no excuses, not even family emergencies. Authorities have already activated a nationwide verification system. Patrol units can now scan a license plate and instantly confirm whether the driver matches the registered owner. If they don't, the vehicle will be seized and the driver will be fined. Officials claim the measure is meant to bring more order and control to the roads but millions of people are already calling it excessive, restrictive and disruptive to everyday life. Beginning November 22nd, something as simple as letting your child, a friend or even a neighbor borrow your car will automatically qualify as a serious violation. There will be no tolerance, no exceptions, no quick appeals. Every entry will be logged digitally and any mismatch will be punished immediately. This new policy is about to impact millions of people quietly and abruptly. Share this message before more people get caught off guard.

Expand article logo  Continue reading



The claim also circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.

The 9 hidden patterns scientists are just beginning to notice
Story by Jeff Blaumberg • 4mo
Animal Behavior Follows a Shared Hidden Algorithm
©Pexels
In a study spanning meerkats in the Kalahari desert, coatis in Panama's rainforest, and spotted hyenas in Kenya's savanna, researchers discovered that the daily actions of these animals show surprisingly similar patterns. These are species that share almost nothing in terms of habitat, diet, or social structure. Yet the underlying rhythm of their behavior is strikingly consistent.

By tracking movement patterns with accelerometers and using machine learning, researchers discovered that the longer an animal stays in one behavior, like resting or foraging, the less likely it is to switch - a pattern known as a "decreasing hazard function." This surprising consistency across species suggests a hidden algorithm shaping behavioral sequences. To the international team of fourteen authors, led by researchers at the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, the findings are unexpected and - possibly - profound.

The 9 hidden patterns scientists are just beginning to notice
Story by Jeff Blaumberg • 4mo
Aging Doesn't Happen Uniformly - Each Organ Runs Its Own Clock
©Pexels
Aging occurs in a heterogeneous manner across different organs, leading to varying risks of chronic diseases and mortality. Biological age offers a more comprehensive reflection of the aging process and is a stronger predictor of disease risk and lifespan. Recent advances in plasma proteomics have enabled the development of organ-specific aging clocks, revealing distinct aging trajectories and their clinical implications.

In other words, your liver may be aging at a completely different rate than your brain - even inside the same body.

Using a tool called EasySci, researchers were able to simultaneously scan more than 21 million cells from every major mouse organ across five stages of life. Their findings reveal that certain cell populations change in every organ, both in the same way and at the same time, during specific stages of life. This suggests that aging is not a linear process but instead a developmental stage sparked by specific molecular cues.

That's a fundamental shift in how scientists think about time inside the body.

Does law make lending someone your car a federal offense starting in November?
Story by Laerke Christensen • 1mo • 4 min read


A white person wearing a blue sweater drops a set of car keys into the hand of a white person wearing a grey top. Getty Images, accessed via Canva
A white person wearing a blue sweater drops a set of car keys into the hand of a white person wearing a grey top. Getty Images, accessed via Canva

Claim:

From Nov. 22, lending your vehicle to a person who is not the registered owner will be a federal offense resulting in a $1000 fine.

Rating:

False (About this rating?)

In July 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that, starting Nov. 22, lending a vehicle to anyone other than the registered owner would be a federal offense resulting in a $1,000 fine.

For example, one Facebook page shared the claim on July 23, 2026. The page's post featured a video with a robotic voice that said: 

Starting November 22, lending your vehicle to anyone will officially be considered a federal offense. The new regulation goes into effect without exceptions and only the person registered on the vehicle's documentation will be legally allowed to drive it. The penalty is immediate — a $1,000 fine on the spot with no warnings, no grace period and no excuses, not even family emergencies. Authorities have already activated a nationwide verification system. Patrol units can now scan a license plate and instantly confirm whether the driver matches the registered owner. If they don't, the vehicle will be seized and the driver will be fined. Officials claim the measure is meant to bring more order and control to the roads but millions of people are already calling it excessive, restrictive and disruptive to everyday life. Beginning November 22nd, something as simple as letting your child, a friend or even a neighbor borrow your car will automatically qualify as a serious violation. There will be no tolerance, no exceptions, no quick appeals. Every entry will be logged digitally and any mismatch will be punished immediately. This new policy is about to impact millions of people quietly and abruptly. Share this message before more people get caught off guard.

The claim also circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.

The 9 hidden patterns scientists are just beginning to notice
Story by Jeff Blaumberg • 4mo
The Brain Starts Being Shaped by Microbes Before Birth
©Unsplash
Scientists at Michigan State University discovered that microbes begin shaping the brain before a baby is born. These microbes affect cells in a part of the brain that controls stress and how we act with other people. It's a finding that challenges the assumption that the microbiome's influence on the brain begins only after birth, once the infant is exposed to the outside world.

The implications stretch far. Scientists have also discovered a crucial connection between gut microbes and anxiety-related behavior, with research suggesting that microbial communities influence stress responses in ways that operate well before conscious experience begins. The gut-brain axis, it turns out, is being written earlier in life than anyone suspected.

The 9 hidden patterns scientists are just beginning to notice
Story by Jeff Blaumberg • 4mo
Nature's Patterns Repeat Across Wildly Different Scales
©Pexels
The natural world is resplendent with patterns - clearly visible intrinsic regularities of form manifest as symmetries, branching fractals, tessellations, waves, meanders, cracks, foams, stripes, and spirals. The logarithmic spiral is a constant feature across a massive range of scales, extending from the fossil dimensions of ammonite shells, through the swirling fury of hurricanes, and upward, to the rotational immensity of stars in a spiral galaxy.

Very often the same types of pattern and form - spirals, stripes, branches, and fractals - recur in places that seem to have nothing in common, as when the markings of a zebra mimic the ripples in windblown sand. Scientists are now using AI to study these repeating geometries more rigorously, and the more precisely they look, the more universal the underlying rules appear to be. New forms of patterns are being discovered almost as fast as we can find explanations.

The 9 hidden patterns scientists are just beginning to notice
Story by Jeff Blaumberg • 4mo
A New Species of Human Ancestor Hidden Inside Old Bones
©Pixabay
In 2025, analyses suggested two ancient skulls might have belonged to Denisovans, shifting our understanding of how we evolved from our ancestors - and what some of those ancestors looked like. Two studies, one in Science and one in Cell, analyzed a well-known 146,000-year-old skull called the Dragon Man, with flat cheeks and prominent facial features, and suggested the fossil belonged to a Denisovan.

Denisovans, early humans first discovered in 2010, share a common ancestor with both Neanderthals and modern humans. Scientists have come to know them primarily from genetic data, because their intact fossils are mostly just bone fragments and teeth. To make this connection, researchers extracted proteins from a bone in the skull's inner ear and DNA from plaque on its teeth - a remarkably intimate piece of detective work on bones that have been in museum collections for years.

The 9 hidden patterns scientists are just beginning to notice
Story by Jeff Blaumberg • 4mo
The Speed of Species Discovery Is Accelerating, Not Slowing
©The Speed of Species Discovery Is Accelerating, Not Slowing (LauraFlohrReynolds, Flickr, CC BY-SA 2.0)
A new study led by researchers at the University of Arizona and published in Science Advances shows that the pace of discovery is accelerating. Today, scientists are identifying more than 16,000 new species each year, the highest rate ever recorded. The researchers say this trend is not slowing and suggest that groups such as plants, fungi, arachnids, fishes, and amphibians are far more diverse than previously believed.

Underground fungi may be one of Earth's most powerful and overlooked allies in the fight against climate change, yet the vast majority of them remain unknown to science. Many species remain undiscovered, especially insects and microbes, and future advances could unlock millions more. Each new find also opens doors to conservation and medical breakthroughs.

The idea that we've already catalogued most of life on Earth is looking less credible with every passing year.

The 9 hidden patterns scientists are just beginning to notice
Story by Jeff Blaumberg • 4mo
Disrupted Sleep Follows a Pattern That Links to Cancer Risk
©Pixabay
The share of colorectal cancer diagnoses among young patients has nearly doubled in the past 30 years, and scientists don't yet know exactly why. A UC Irvine study finds that inconsistent sleep habits could be part of the problem. Mice with genetically disturbed sleep had less diverse and abundant bacteria in their gut and produced less protective intestinal mucus - two conditions that are correlated with higher risk of tumor growth.

Staying up late, pulling all-nighters, and even midnight snacking could produce similar effects by disrupting the body's internal clock. What's emerging is a consistent pattern: circadian disruption doesn't just make you tired. It quietly reorganizes the gut's biological environment in ways that may take years to become visible.

The clock and the microbiome, it turns out, are deeply entangled.

Does law make lending someone your car a federal offense starting in November?
Story by Laerke Christensen • 1mo • 4 min read


A white person wearing a blue sweater drops a set of car keys into the hand of a white person wearing a grey top. Getty Images, accessed via Canva
A white person wearing a blue sweater drops a set of car keys into the hand of a white person wearing a grey top. Getty Images, accessed via Canva

Claim:

From Nov. 22, lending your vehicle to a person who is not the registered owner will be a federal offense resulting in a $1000 fine.

Rating:

False (About this rating?)

In July 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that, starting Nov. 22, lending a vehicle to anyone other than the registered owner would be a federal offense resulting in a $1,000 fine.

For example, one Facebook page shared the claim on July 23, 2026. The page's post featured a video with a robotic voice that said: 

Starting November 22, lending your vehicle to anyone will officially be considered a federal offense. The new regulation goes into effect without exceptions and only the person registered on the vehicle's documentation will be legally allowed to drive it. The penalty is immediate — a $1,000 fine on the spot with no warnings, no grace period and no excuses, not even family emergencies. Authorities have already activated a nationwide verification system. Patrol units can now scan a license plate and instantly confirm whether the driver matches the registered owner. If they don't, the vehicle will be seized and the driver will be fined. Officials claim the measure is meant to bring more order and control to the roads but millions of people are already calling it excessive, restrictive and disruptive to everyday life. Beginning November 22nd, something as simple as letting your child, a friend or even a neighbor borrow your car will automatically qualify as a serious violation. There will be no tolerance, no exceptions, no quick appeals. Every entry will be logged digitally and any mismatch will be punished immediately. This new policy is about to impact millions of people quietly and abruptly. Share this message before more people get caught off guard.

The 9 hidden patterns scientists are just beginning to notice
Story by Jeff Blaumberg • 4mo
Whales Communicate in Structured Patterns Across Species Boundaries
©Pexels
Whale researchers dropped a microphone into the seas off southeast Alaska and recorded a humpback making a "whup"-like noise - roughly a humpback hello. The next day, they lowered a speaker into the water and played the recorded call back as a pod of whales passed by. One whale, a middle-aged female named Twain, responded in kind.

For 20 minutes, Twain and the scientists exchanged calls 36 times in a row. Researchers even varied the timing of their calls and Twain matched their tempo.

The structured, turn-taking nature of the exchange points to something that looks less like simple noise and more like a recognizable communication pattern - one with rhythm, reciprocity, and timing. Astrophysicists with the SETI Institute, which searches for extraterrestrial life, are developing algorithms that can quantify the complexity of such animal communication to understand what kinds of signals might indicate intelligence anywhere in the universe. Humpback whales, it seems, may have something to teach us about how to listen.

Profile Picture

pexels-ron-lach-10186702
pexels-ron-lach-10186702
© Ron Lach/pexels.com
A team of physicists at Oak Ridge National Laboratory has resolved a long-standing puzzle in quantum materials research: why do two honeycomb-lattice magnets with identical crystal structures behave so differently when cooled and reheated? Their answer — published September 3, 2026, in Physical Review Materials and selected as an Editors' Suggestion — carries direct consequences for anyone building quantum computing or spintronic devices out of two-dimensional magnetic materials.

Online Courses For Adults
Online Courses For Adults
University of Phoenix
·
Sponsored
call to action icon
Chromium trichloride (CrCl₃) and alpha-ruthenium trichloride (α-RuCl₃) are, on a crystal-structure diagram, virtually indistinguishable: both belong to the layered transition-metal trihalide family, both host metal ions at the vertices of a honeycomb lattice, and both undergo the same type of temperature-driven structural rearrangement as they are cooled from room temperature. Yet in practice, CrCl₃ is structurally robust — it cycles through that rearrangement gracefully and recovers — while α-RuCl₃ progressively degrades with each cycle, accumulating stacking faults that alter its magnetic ordering temperature, suppress its thermal conductivity, and make its experimental behavior nearly impossible to reproduce from laboratory to laboratory.

The study, led by Zachary Morgan of ORNL's Neutron Scattering Division together with Iris Ye, Jiasen Guo, and materials scientists Michael A. McGuire and Jiaqiang Yan, used neutron single-crystal diffraction at the Spallation Neutron Source to track both materials simultaneously through their structural transitions — the first direct, side-by-side comparison of this kind on single crystals of both compounds.

AI Music Creator: Songer
AI Music Creator: Songer
Songer
Songer
·
Sponsored
call to action icon
Why the Crystal Matters: A Primer on Honeycomb Magnets
In a transition-metal trihalide, metal ions — chromium in CrCl₃, ruthenium in α-RuCl₃ — sit at the vertices of a honeycomb lattice inside each layer. Those layers are stacked on top of one another and held together not by strong chemical bonds but by weak van der Waals forces: the same gentle intermolecular attraction that allows graphite to flake off onto paper.

That weak interlayer coupling is what makes these materials so attractive for device engineering. It allows layers to be mechanically peeled away to atomically thin sheets, which can then be reassembled into heterostructures — layered sandwiches of different two-dimensional materials assembled like atomic-scale building blocks. Chromium trihalides including CrCl₃ have already been demonstrated as spin-filter magnetic tunnel junctions with tunneling magnetoresistance values ranging from 17,000% to 57,000%, opening a route toward voltage-controlled magnetic memory.

But weak coupling also means the stacking arrangement is energetically fragile. At high temperature, both CrCl₃ and α-RuCl₃ adopt a monoclinic structure in which adjacent layers are offset in a near-face-centered-cubic pattern. On cooling, both transition to a rhombohedral structure in which the layers adopt a different lateral offset — closer to hexagonal close-packing. This first-order structural phase transition, driven by the collective sliding of layers relative to one another, reshuffles the exchange pathways through which magnetic interactions are transmitted between layers.

The central question the ORNL team set out to answer: does that reshuffling happen the same way in both materials, and does it couple to magnetism the same way?

What ORNL's Neutrons Revealed
To answer that question, the team used neutron single-crystal diffraction — the technique of choice for probing both crystal structure and magnetic order simultaneously, because neutrons carry their own magnetic moment and scatter from both atomic and magnetic arrangements. By tracking Bragg peaks (sharp reflections from long-range crystalline order) and diffuse scattering (broader, smeared intensity from short-range correlations or disorder) as the temperature swept through the transition range, they could watch each material rearrange and document what happened on either side of the transition.

The contrast was stark.

CrCl₃ handled the transition smoothly. Its in-plane lattice parameter — the spacing between chromium ions within a single honeycomb plane — evolved continuously and without any abrupt jump as the temperature passed through the transition. The structural changes were reversible: heat the crystal through the transition, cool it back down, and it returned to essentially the same state it started from, with no progressive accumulation of damage across repeated cycles.

Magnetically, CrCl₃ ordered into an A-type antiferromagnetic structure at a Néel temperature of 14 K — a configuration in which adjacent honeycomb planes align their spins antiparallel, while spins within each plane align ferromagnetically. But what stood out was what happened above that ordering temperature: diffuse magnetic scattering — the neutron signature of short-range spin correlations — persisted all the way up to roughly 40 K, some 26 degrees above the point where true long-range magnetic order snaps into place. CrCl₃'s spins remain correlated and locally organized long before they commit to global magnetic order.

α-RuCl₃ told the opposite story. Its in-plane lattice parameter did not evolve smoothly — it jumped discontinuously across the structural transition, showing pronounced hysteresis between the heating and cooling legs of the same thermal cycle. More critically, repeating the cycle caused the crystal to progressively degrade. Each thermal trip accumulated stacking faults that did not heal on cooling — a ratchet-like buildup of crystalline disorder.

Magnetically, α-RuCl₃ showed a complete absence of diffuse scattering above its ordering temperature of 7.6 K. Where CrCl₃'s spins remained correlated far above T_N, those in α-RuCl₃ appeared to disengage abruptly at the ordering temperature, leaving no short-range magnetic precursor.

What Is the Structural Transition, and Why Does It Differ?
The key to understanding the contrast lies in the fundamentally different electronic characters of chromium and ruthenium in these compounds.

Chromium in CrCl₃ is a 3d transition metal — a lighter element — with three electrons in its d-shell, all with parallel spins. Its magnetic interactions are dominated by conventional Heisenberg-type exchange: isotropic, relatively short-ranged, and insensitive to the precise geometry of the crystal lattice beyond nearest-neighbor distances. When CrCl₃ layers slide into a new stacking configuration during the structural transition, the magnetic exchange pathways shift, but the Heisenberg exchange adapts smoothly. The in-plane bonds do not need to strain abruptly to accommodate the new configuration.

Ruthenium in α-RuCl₃ is a 4d metal — heavier — and its greater atomic number brings strong spin-orbit coupling into play. Spin-orbit coupling is the relativistic interaction between an electron's spin and its orbital motion; in heavier elements like ruthenium, it is strong enough to fundamentally entangle spin and orbital degrees of freedom into a new effective quantum number (J_eff = 1/2).

This is precisely what makes α-RuCl₃ famous: it is one of the leading candidate materials for realizing a Kitaev quantum spin liquid — a theoretically predicted state, solved exactly by mathematician Alexei Kitaev in 2006, in which spins on a honeycomb lattice are so highly entangled that they never magnetically order, instead hosting exotic fractionalized excitations called Majorana fermions. The 2019 review of Kitaev materials by Takagi, Takayama, Jackeli, Khaliullin, and Nagler provides a comprehensive account of the concept and its material realizations.

The magnetic interactions that produce this state — the Kitaev couplings — are bond-dependent and highly anisotropic: each of the three types of bonds in the honeycomb lattice carries a different spin component interaction. This means the interactions are exquisitely sensitive to the precise geometry of the ruthenium-chloride-ruthenium exchange pathways — and hence to the exact layer stacking. When α-RuCl₃ layers slide during the structural transition, the resulting change in exchange pathway geometry is not something the in-plane lattice can accommodate elastically. The abrupt jump in the in-plane lattice parameter — and the progressive damage — is the mechanical consequence of that geometric sensitivity.

In CrCl₃, by contrast, the Heisenberg-dominated exchange imposes no equivalent geometric constraint. Layers slide, the stacking rearranges, and the in-plane bonds remain unperturbed.

Why This Is Costing Quantum Computing Researchers Sleep
The structural fragility of α-RuCl₃ is not merely an inconvenience for experimentalists. It is the root cause of one of the most consequential reproducibility problems in contemporary condensed matter physics.

For the past decade, α-RuCl₃ has been the community's best bet for observing Majorana fermions in a material setting — not as individual exotic particles in expensive cryogenic setups, but as collective excitations in a relatively ordinary-looking black crystal. Topological quantum computers would use Majorana fermions to store information in a form that is inherently resistant to decoherence: rather than isolating a qubit from its environment (the conventional approach), topological quantum computing would encode information in the global entanglement pattern of the spin liquid itself, making it robust to any local perturbation.

The smoking-gun signature of that state is a half-quantized thermal Hall conductance — a precise fractional value that emerges from Majorana edge modes when a magnetic field is applied to α-RuCl₃. Several research groups have reported seeing this half-quantized value. Several others have not been able to reproduce it, or have measured values that fall far short of quantization — a controversy documented in preprint form and debated actively across the field.

Prior ORNL work published in Physical Review Materials in 2024 — by McGuire, Yan, and co-workers, several of whom are also authors on the current study — showed that the thermal Hall conductance measurement in α-RuCl₃ is strongly sample-dependent, and that samples with more stacking disorder systematically show lower values that push the measured result further from the half-quantized target. Crystals with minimal stacking disorder show higher thermal conductivity and a thermal Hall conductance that approaches the predicted quantized value.

The current study explains why stacking disorder accumulates in α-RuCl₃: the abrupt in-plane lattice jump during the first-order structural transition generates elastic strains that damage the crystal's layer stacking — and that damage adds up with every thermal cycle a sample undergoes during growth, post-growth annealing, or repeated experimental cycling. CrCl₃ does not have this problem because its Heisenberg-dominated exchange does not lock the in-plane bonds to the stacking geometry the way Kitaev coupling does in α-RuCl₃.

In other words: the property that makes α-RuCl₃ scientifically extraordinary — the bond-directional, spin-orbit-driven Kitaev exchange — is the same property that makes its crystals mechanically fragile. The exotic physics and the structural weakness share a common root.

What Are the Structural Transitions, Exactly?
Both CrCl₃ and α-RuCl₃ switch between two well-defined crystal structures as they pass through the structural transition. At high temperature, both adopt a monoclinic arrangement (space group C2/m), in which adjacent honeycomb layers are offset from one another by a lateral displacement that corresponds roughly to face-centered-cubic layer ordering. On cooling below the transition temperature — which occurs near 240 K (−33°F) for CrCl₃ and near 150 K (−189°F) for α-RuCl₃ — both switch to a rhombohedral arrangement (space group R3̄), in which the lateral displacement corresponds to a different close-packed ordering.

The difference the ORNL team documented is in how that switching happens in the two materials. In CrCl₃, the lattice breathes smoothly through the change. In α-RuCl₃, the abruptness of the transition — visible as a discontinuous jump in the in-plane lattice parameter, and as a pronounced difference between the heating and cooling curves — is the mechanical signature of a system whose in-plane bonding chemistry is being pulled into conflict with its stacking geometry as the layers try to slide.

The c-lattice parameter (the spacing between layers, measured perpendicular to the honeycomb planes) shows a step-like change in both materials — consistent with the expected stacking rearrangement. It is the in-plane response that diverges, and that divergence is the key finding.

What This Tells Device Engineers
For researchers building spintronic devices from van der Waals magnetic layers, the study's message is straightforward: structural reversibility under thermal cycling cannot be assumed from crystal-structure analogy alone.

CrCl₃ and its chromium trihalide relatives — CrBr₃ and CrI₃ — have attracted intense interest as magnetic layers in van der Waals heterostructure devices. In those architectures, a magnetic CrX₃ layer sandwiched between graphene contacts creates an atomically thin spin filter: switching the magnetization state of the CrX₃ layer changes the tunneling resistance dramatically, enabling voltage-controlled magnetic memory and logic without traditional magnetic materials. The ORNL result validates CrCl₃'s suitability for those applications by confirming that it cycles through its structural transition cleanly and without accumulating disorder that would unpredictably shift its magnetic switching behavior. Research on CrCl₃ flakes to monolayer thickness further supports the path toward scalable device manufacturing.

For α-RuCl₃ and topological quantum computing, the implications are more sobering in the short term. The progressive stacking disorder accumulation means that samples degrade with use, making sample selection, preparation, and characterization not incidental to the experiment but central to it. The ORNL team's prior work established criteria for selecting minimal-disorder crystals: a structural transition near 140 K on cooling, and a single magnetic anomaly near 7.6 K in specific heat. The new study explains the mechanism behind those criteria — a crystal that shows the transition cleanly near 140 K has not yet accumulated the in-plane strain damage that pushes the transition temperature down and smears it.

More broadly, the study establishes that in van der Waals magnets, structural analogy does not imply functional equivalence: materials with the same space group and the same nominal crystal architecture can differ fundamentally in how their layers respond to thermal stress, and how that stress couples back to magnetic behavior. For quantum device engineering, where reproducibility is not a statistical luxury but an operational requirement, the coupling between structural mechanics and electronic configuration is a design variable that must be tested explicitly.

How Neutron Diffraction Made This Visible
The methodological choice at the heart of the study — neutron single-crystal diffraction using the CORELLI elastic diffuse scattering spectrometer at ORNL's Spallation Neutron Source — was critical to the findings. Neutrons interact with both the nuclear and magnetic structure of a material in a single experiment, allowing the team to track structural and magnetic order simultaneously as a function of temperature, rather than running separate measurements that might reflect slightly different sample conditions.

The ability to distinguish Bragg peaks (which carry information about the long-range crystalline order) from diffuse scattering (which reveals departures from that order — stacking faults, short-range correlations, and disordered domains) gave the team direct access to the disorder that is invisible to conventional X-ray diffraction but critical to the physical properties being debated.

Frequently Asked Questions
What is a Kitaev quantum spin liquid, and why does it matter for quantum computing?
A Kitaev quantum spin liquid is a state of matter predicted by mathematician Alexei Kitaev in 2006, in which spins on a honeycomb lattice are quantum mechanically entangled in a specific topological pattern without ever settling into ordinary magnetic order. The excitations of this state — called Majorana fermions — obey a type of quantum statistics (non-Abelian anyons under a magnetic field) that could be used to store and process quantum information in a form that is inherently resistant to the environmental disturbances that cause ordinary qubits to fail. Alpha-ruthenium trichloride (α-RuCl₃) is currently the most studied material candidate for hosting this state.

Why has α-RuCl₃ been so difficult to study reproducibly across different laboratories?
Multiple research groups have reported conflicting measurements of the same key property — the thermal Hall conductance, which should show a precise half-integer quantized value if Majorana fermions are present. Prior ORNL work established that the measurement is strongly sample-dependent: crystals with more stacking disorder (layers offset from their ideal positions) produce lower thermal conductivity and measurements that fall further from the predicted quantized value. The new Morgan et al. study explains why stacking disorder accumulates in α-RuCl₃: the abrupt, hysteretic jump in the in-plane lattice parameter during the structural transition generates elastic damage that adds up with each thermal cycle. This structural explanation for the reproducibility problem is a significant advance.

What makes CrCl₃ a better candidate for van der Waals spintronic devices than α-RuCl₃?
CrCl₃'s magnetism is governed by isotropic Heisenberg exchange, which is not geometrically sensitive to the precise stacking arrangement of the honeycomb layers. As a result, CrCl₃ cycles through its structural phase transition smoothly — the in-plane lattice parameter evolves continuously, with no abrupt jump, and the crystal does not accumulate damage. This structural reversibility means CrCl₃ can withstand the thermal cycling inherent in device manufacturing and repeated operation without progressively shifting its magnetic properties — a requirement that α-RuCl₃, which degrades with each cycle, cannot currently meet. Research on growing CrCl₃ to monolayer thickness confirms its promise for scalable spintronic applications.

What is diffuse magnetic scattering, and what does the difference between the two materials tell us?
Diffuse magnetic scattering is the broad, spread-out neutron signal that arises when spins in a material are correlated over short distances — organizing themselves into local patches of order — without yet committing to the long-range, fully-ordered magnetic state. In CrCl₃, this diffuse scattering persists up to about 40 K, roughly 26 K above the temperature at which true long-range magnetic order locks in at 14 K. That persistence reflects the gradual, isotropic nature of Heisenberg exchange: spins build up local coherence progressively over a wide temperature range before snapping into global order. In α-RuCl₃, no equivalent diffuse scattering was detected above the 7.6 K ordering temperature — consistent with the anisotropic, bond-directional Kitaev exchange, which suppresses the conventional precursor fluctuations that CrCl₃'s Heisenberg exchange readily supports.

The nature of time has plagued thinkers for as long as we've tried to understand the world we live in. Intuitively, we know what time is, but try to explain it, and we end up tying our minds in knots.

St. Augustine of Hippo, a theologian whose writings influenced western philosophy, captured a paradoxical challenge in trying to articulate time more than 1,600 years ago: "What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to a questioner, I do not know."

Nearly a thousand years earlier, Heraclitus of Ephesus offered a penetrating insight. According to classical Greek philosopher Plato's Cratylus: "Heraclitus is supposed to say that all things are in motion and nothing at rest; he compares them to the stream of a river, and says that you cannot go into the same water twice."

Superficially, this can sound like another paradox—how can something be the same river and yet not the same? But Heraclitus adds clarity, not confusion: the river—a thing that exists—continuously changes. While it is the same river, different waters flow by moment to moment.

While the river's continuous flux makes this plain, the same is true of anything that exists—including the person stepping into the river. They remain the same person, but each moment they set foot in the river is distinct.

How can time feel so obvious, so woven into the fabric of our experience, and yet remain the bane of every thinker who has tried to explain it?

An issue of articulation
The key issue isn't one most physicists would even consider relevant. Nor is it a challenge that philosophers have managed to resolve.

Expand article logo  Continue reading

Time itself isn't difficult to grasp: we all understand it, despite our persistent struggle to describe it. As Augustine sensed, the problem is one of articulation: a failure to precisely draw the right boundaries around the nature of time both conceptually and linguistically.

Specifically, physicists and philosophers tend to conflate what it means for something to exist and what it means for something to happen—treating occurrences as if they exist. Once that distinction is recognized, the fog clears and Augustine's paradox dissolves.

Chinese scientists explain one-way flow of time and why past travel is impossible
Story by Prabhat Ranjan Mishra • 8mo • 3 min read


Chinese scientists explain one-way flow of time and why past travel is impossible
Chinese scientists explain one-way flow of time and why past travel is impossible
Researchers in China have proposed a theory explaining why time moves only forward. Scientists from Hainan University in southern China proposed a new theoretical framework that sheds light on this subject.

New study shows wormholes aren’t tunnels, and the Big Bang was a bounce
Story by Rupendra Brahambhatt • 7mo • 4 min read


New study shows wormholes aren’t tunnels, and the Big Bang was a bounce
New study shows wormholes aren’t tunnels, and the Big Bang was a bounce
For decades, wormholes have been hypothesized as mysterious tunnels that might let us cross galaxies or even time itself—but what if this picture is completely wrong? New study suggests that one of physics’ most famous “wormhole” ideas was never about travel at all. 

Instead, it may be a hidden mirror of time itself. By revisiting a concept introduced by Albert Einstein nearly 90 years ago, the study authors have proposed a new way to reconcile gravity with quantum mechanics—and possibly even rethink what the Big Bang really was.

Online Courses For Adults
Online Courses For Adults
University of Phoenix
·
Sponsored
call to action icon
They have tried to combine Einstein’s theory of gravity, one of the deepest unsolved problems in physics. These two frameworks work extremely well on their own, yet they clash when pushed to extremes, such as inside black holes or at the birth of the universe. 

The new study argues that the solution may have been hiding in plain sight, inside a long-misunderstood idea called the Einstein–Rosen bridge.

The curious case of the Einstein-Rosen bridge
In 1935, Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen were not thinking about wormholes or cosmic highways. They were trying to fix a problem in how particles and gravity were described together.

Their “bridge” was a mathematical construction that linked two perfectly symmetrical copies of spacetime. It was designed to keep physical equations consistent, not to allow anything to pass through. 

Decades later, physicists rebranded this idea as a wormhole, imagining it as a tunnel between distant regions of space. However, detailed calculations showed that such tunnels collapse too quickly to be crossed. So, within standard general relativity, Einstein–Rosen bridges are unstable and unobservable.

Despite this, the wormhole image took on a life of its own in popular culture and speculative physics. The new study goes back to the original problem Einstein and Rosen were tackling and reinterprets it using modern ideas from quantum theory—especially how time works at the smallest scales. 

“This new understanding of the Einstein-Rosen (ER) bridges is not related to classical wormholes, it addresses the original ER puzzle and promises a unitary description of quantum field theory in curved spacetime (QFTCS),” the study authors note.

Wormholes are not tunnels
Most fundamental physical laws do not care whether time runs forward or backward. If you reverse time in the equations, they still work. This symmetry is usually ignored because, in everyday life, time clearly moves in one direction.

The researchers argue that at the microscopic level, especially near black holes or in extreme cosmic environments, this one-way view of time is incomplete. Instead, a full quantum description must include two components: one where time moves forward, and another where it moves backward in a mirror-like fashion. 

Tirzepatide: The GLP1 That Crushes It
Tirzepatide: The GLP1 That Crushes It
Direct Meds GLP-1
Direct Meds GLP-1

Sponsored
call to action icon
The Einstein–Rosen bridge, in this view, is not a tunnel through space. It is a mathematical connection between these two opposite arrows of time. This reinterpretation has powerful consequences. 

“These mathematical bridges not only retain the vision of ER, but also restore the unitarity in curved spacetime,” the study authors added.

For instance, one of the biggest puzzles in physics is the black hole information paradox. In the 1970s, Stephen Hawking showed that black holes emit radiation and can eventually evaporate, seemingly destroying all information about what fell into them. This violates a core rule of quantum mechanics, which says information must always be preserved.

The paradox arises because physicists usually describe black holes using only one direction of time. In the new framework, information is not destroyed at the event horizon. Instead, it continues evolving along the mirror, time-reversed component of the quantum state. 

They're Like Walking On A Soft Cloud- Now 70% Off!

loomhe

Sponsored
call to action icon
From our perspective, it disappears—but at the fundamental level, nothing is lost. The laws of quantum mechanics remain intact, without requiring exotic matter or radical changes to Einstein’s theory.

How this affects black holes, the Big Bang, and the universe itself
If this picture is correct, its implications go far beyond black holes. For instance, the same time-mirror structure could apply to the entire universe. The Big Bang may not have been the absolute beginning of time, but a quantum “bounce”—a transition between a contracting universe and an expanding one, each with opposite arrows of time.

In this scenario, our universe could be the interior of a black hole formed in a previous cosmos. As that region collapsed, quantum effects prevented a final singularity, causing spacetime to rebound and expand again. 

Some traces of the pre-bounce universe—such as small black holes—might have survived and reappeared in our own cosmic expansion. Intriguingly, such relics could help explain part of what we currently call dark matter.

However, this idea remains theoretical. It does not predict sci-fi wormholes, faster-than-light travel, or time machines. Testing it will require new ways to connect quantum theory, cosmology, and observations of black holes and the early universe. 

The researchers now aim to refine the mathematical framework and identify clearer observational signatures that could confirm—or falsify—the picture.

The study is published in the journal Classical and Quantum Gravity.

MIT physicists show why a laser made of neutrinos is impossible
Story by Joseph Shavit • 1w • 6 min read

MIT physicists conclude that a proposed neutrino laser based on an ultracold radioactive gas cannot produce the superradiant amplification needed for a beam.
One analysis finds that violent atomic recoil destroys the quantum coherence needed for amplification, while another shows that neutrinos’ fermionic nature blocks the required emission cascade.
The result overturns a 2025 proposal that suggested a condensate of radioactive rubidium could shorten an 86-day decay lifetime to about one minute.
A laser made from some of the universe’s most elusive particles sounded almost too strange to be possible. According to two new theoretical analyses from MIT, it is.

The LA Recording School - A Division of LA Film School - Music Production Degree Online
The LA Recording School - A Division of LA Film School - Music Production Degree Online
Los Angeles Film School
Los Angeles Film School
·
Sponsored
call to action icon
Physicists have found that a recently proposed neutrino laser cannot achieve the collective amplification needed to turn radioactive decay into a concentrated beam. Two companion papers published in Physical Review Letters identify separate problems with the concept: the enormous recoil produced when a neutrino escapes an atom, and the fundamentally fermionic nature of the neutrino itself.

“These two papers are sort of punch one and punch two,” MIT physicist Wolfgang Ketterle said. “Each paper would have killed the proposal.”

The work was carried out by Ketterle, postdoctoral researchers Hanzhen Lin and Yu-Kun Lu, and colleagues at MIT’s Department of Physics, Research Laboratory of Electronics and MIT-Harvard Center for Ultracold Atoms. The findings do not show that every imaginable method of producing directional neutrinos is impossible. Instead, they rule out the specific superradiant mechanism proposed for radioactive Bose-Einstein condensates.


In the neutrino-laser scheme proposed in 2025, each rubidium atom in a Bose-Einstein condensate decays into a krypton atom and a neutrino. (CREDIT: APS/Carin Cain)
In the neutrino-laser scheme proposed in 2025, each rubidium atom in a Bose-Einstein condensate decays into a krypton atom and a neutrino. (CREDIT: APS/Carin Cain)
An audacious proposal for ghost particles
Neutrinos barely interact with ordinary matter. Trillions pass through the human body every second, yet detecting even a small fraction requires enormous, highly sensitive experiments. They also come in different varieties, or flavors, and can change from one flavor into another while traveling.

Related video: Scientists found a particle 6 times more powerful than physics allowed (Sciencephile the AI)

Sciencephile the AI
Scientists found a particle 6 times more powerful than physics allowed
Hello mortals.
