Scientists are one step closer to understanding the origins of complex life on Earth after shedding new light on a mystery about our microbial ancestors. The key, they suspect, may lie in how simple microbes that lived billions of years ago adapted to the presence of oxygen.

Humans, like all plants, fungi and animals on Earth, are eukaryotes — organisms with cells that have a clearly defined DNA-containing nucleus and other structures such as mitochondria, organelles that provide cells with power by converting nutrients into energy.

Online Courses For Adults
Online Courses For Adults
University of Phoenix
·
Sponsored
call to action icon
Between 2.4 billion and 2.1 billion years ago, oxygen levels dramatically increased in Earth’s atmosphere, known as the Great Oxidation Event. A few hundred thousand years after the event, the first identifiable traces of eukaryotes, preserved as microfossils, appeared on our planet, suggesting that oxygen has long been a crucial ingredient for the evolution of complex life.

Many scientists believe that eukaryotes evolved from the combination of two types of microbes.

But in a puzzling twist, one of the microbes, known as Asgard archaea, has only been found in oxygen-deprived environments such as hydrothermal vents on the ocean floor — despite appearing to share complex similarities with eukaryotes.

Researchers have questioned how Asgards even crossed paths with other microbes that required oxygen for survival to create eukaryotes if they existed in such different environments.

How a Classic Fantasy RPG Continues to Evolve Its Gameplay
How a Classic Fantasy RPG Continues to Evolve Its Gameplay
Loot Horizon
·
Sponsored
call to action icon
But a new investigation of Asgard genomes has revealed previously unknown lineages of the microbes in shallow coastal sediments, some of which appear tolerant of and use oxygen, according to a study published February 18 in the journal Nature.

“The fact that some of the Asgards, which are our ancestors, were able to use oxygen fits in with this very well,” study coauthor Brett Baker, associate professor of marine science and integrative biology at the University of Texas at Austin, said in a statement. “Oxygen appeared in the environment, and Asgards adapted to that. They found an energetic advantage to using oxygen, and then they evolved into eukaryotes.”

Understanding the role of Asgards in the development of complex life could help solve the bigger mystery of how exactly microbes evolved into eukaryotes — and why we’re all here, Baker said.

AI Music Creator: Songer
AI Music Creator: Songer
Songer
Songer
·
Sponsored
call to action icon
A microbe with mythological roots
Asgard archaea, named for the celestial home of Norse gods such as Odin and Thor, is a superphylum, or a group that evolved from a common ancestor.

A single phylum within this group was first discovered in 2015 near an underwater volcano in the North Atlantic Ocean known as Loki’s Castle due to its resemblance to the horned helmet worn by the Marvel Comics character — who also happens to be a god in Norse mythology. The microbe was dubbed Lokiarchaeota.

Other phyla of Asgard microbes have also been named after gods from Norse mythology.

When compared with microbes in other superphyla, Asgards appear to be closely related to eukaryotes and contain genes only seen in complex life.

“They were hailed as sort of the missing link in the evolution of life, from single-celled microbial life to complex life like plants and animals,” Baker told CNN.

By examining samples from a broad range of environments, researchers are increasingly finding more types of Asgard microbes, such as Heimdallarchaeia, named for the guardian of Asgard.

In 2023, Baker and his colleagues found that eukaryotes appear most closely related to the Heimdall group of Asgard microbes, which have high-energy metabolic pathways. The findings supported the idea that animals and other life forms must get the most energy from breathing oxygen and bolstered the theory that a rise in oxygen on Earth correlated with the appearance of complex life, Baker said.

The next step was to understand what energy-generating processes could unfold in different types of Asgard microbes based on their genes.

To investigate this question, Baker and his colleagues carried out large-scale DNA sequencing from samples collected in deep-sea hydrothermal vents as well as shallow coastal areas. The team was able to gather hundreds of previously unknown genomes and build a tree of life for Asgard microbes by comparing genetic similarities and differences between the microbes within the superphylum.


Asgard microbes were found in mud samples taken from the Guaymas Basin in the Gulf of California. - Brett Baker/National Science Foundation
Asgard microbes were found in mud samples taken from the Guaymas Basin in the Gulf of California. - Brett Baker/National Science Foundation
Previously unknown protein groups in the microbes were uncovered while assembling the Asgard family tree, enabling Baker and his colleagues to compare the proteins with those used by eukaryotes to generate energy and metabolize oxygen. An artificial intelligence model helped the team identify how the proteins can fold into different structures, which correlates with how they function.

Several proteins produced by Heimdall microbes are similar to eukaryotic proteins that process oxygen to efficiently generate energy, suggesting that at least some ancient Asgards may have been oxygen-tolerant.

Uncovering an ancient ancestor
At first, scientists thought the ancient microbial ancestor of complex life was a simple cell, dwelling in oxygen-free environments.

That cell, they theorized, adapted to use oxygen after combining with a bacterium, eventually giving rise to the presence of mitochondria in our cells.

“Eukaryotes almost always rely on mitochondria to burn hydrocarbons in oxygen to do all the amazing things we do,” Buzz Baum, cell biologist and group leader of the Baum Lab at the Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, England, wrote in an email. Baum did not participate in the new study.

But the new findings suggest that Asgards might have already adapted to process oxygen before combining with bacteria. This tolerance would have placed Asgards in oxygenated environments and might have helped facilitate their merger with bacteria, according to the study.


The research submersible Alvin was used to search the deep ocean for Asgard microbes. - Brett Baker/National Science Foundation
The research submersible Alvin was used to search the deep ocean for Asgard microbes. - Brett Baker/National Science Foundation
“The transition to complex life didn’t require innovating oxygen metabolism from scratch — the building blocks were already there,” wrote Burak Avci, assistant professor of microbiology at Denmark’s Aarhaus University, in an email. Avci was not involved in the new research.

“However, it is important to recognize that we are examining modern-day representatives of an ancient event that occurred billions of years ago,” he said. “There is a significant evolutionary time gap, and the actual encounters of this event may have involved different metabolic strategies in forming the first eukaryotic cell.”

The study authors also noted that more evidence is needed to biologically confirm the genetic predictions in the study, especially when trying to determine the exact capabilities of ancient Asgards from almost 2 billion years ago.

Modern Asgards have likely changed and adapted to use oxygen, Baum noted.

The study adds to a growing body of evidence that eukaryotic cells originated in oxygen-containing coastal environments, said Daniel Brady Mills, postdoctoral researcher in the Institute of Molecular Evolution at Germany’s University of Düsseldorf. Mills, who was not involved in the research, said he hopes the study will inspire others to culture their own specimens in lab settings to test whether or not Asgard microbes can use oxygen.

Baker is hopeful that scientists will reach a milestone within the next five to 10 years: observing the evolution of lab-grown Asgard microbes as they turn into eukaryotic cells, a process known as eukaryogenesis.

“There’s no reason to think that this only happened once 2 billion years ago,” Baker said.

Future studies should also measure the amount of oxygen in the environments where Asgards are present and identify microbes within the superphylum that can grow with only small amounts of oxygen, Baum said.

Asgards are humanity’s closest living relatives from an ancient event, which means they hold clues to our origins, Baum said, so it’s crucial to determine when they began using oxygen.

“If you look around, our planet is dominated by eukaryotes,” Baker said. “Understanding how they formed is a huge transition in the evolution of life on Earth. The fact that we found oxygen in our close ancestors, in Asgards, sort of fits that puzzle really well.”

Most complex mathematical equations ever solved
Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
Fermat's Last Theorem
©DepositPhotos
No solution exists. That’s what Pierre de Fermat claimed in 1637 about the equation x^n + y^n = z^n for integer values greater than 2.

He scribbled a note in his copy of an ancient Greek text, saying he had a proof but the margin was too narrow to contain it.

For 358 years, mathematicians tried to prove him right. The equation became mathematical legend—simple enough for a high school student to understand, impossible enough to defeat the greatest minds in history.

Andrew Wiles finally cracked it in 1995 using techniques that didn’t exist in Fermat’s time. Whatever proof Fermat thought he had, it wasn’t this one.

What Tennessee school board's 2025 policy change means for Pride flag displays
Story by Joey Esposito • 1mo • 5 min read


An American flag is shown in front of a rainbow. K.C. Alfred / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images
An American flag is shown in front of a rainbow. K.C. Alfred / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images

Claim:

A Tennessee school board voted to enact a policy that banned LGBTQ+ Pride flags and allowed only the United States flag or Tennessee state flag to hang in public schools.

Rating:

Mostly True (About this rating?)

What's True:

The Tullahoma City Schools Board of Education voted to change the district's policy regarding flags and other displays such as "banners, pennants, digital signs, etc." in October 2025. The policy effectively restricted any displays to that of the American flag or Tennessee flag unless "directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program."

 
What's False:

The policy does not call for a ban or removal of Pride flags specifically (although the issue stemmed from complaints about a teacher who displayed a Pride flag in their classroom and was explicitly mentioned as the cause of the discussion within the meeting during which the policy was voted on).

 
A rumor that a school board in Tennessee voted in favor of removing LGBTQ+ Pride flags from public schools swirled online in July 2026. 

People on social media posted about the alleged policy change and claimed the school board voted to allow only flags for the United States and the state of Tennessee. 


View this post on Instagram


In sum, the claim was mostly true. During a Tullahoma City Schools Board of Education meeting on Oct. 21, 2025, the board voted to enact a policy that effectively restricted any displays of flags to the American flag or Tennessee state flag unless "directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program."

The policy does not include language calling for a ban or removal of Pride flags specifically. However, the issue stemmed from complaints about a teacher who displayed a Pride flag in their classroom and was explicitly mentioned as the cause of the discussion during the board meeting in which the policy was voted on.

Expand article logo  Continue reading

During the meeting, which is available to view on the school board's website, the policy passed unanimously. The voting on what is referred to as "Board Policy 4.400" can be seen at the 1:22:00 mark. 

The policy, which was read during the board meeting at the 1:07:00 mark, stated in full: 

In order to regulate flags and other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.) on any/all campuses within Tullahoma City Schools and to ensure a conducive and respectful educational environment, the following guidelines have been established:

1. No flag or other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.) other than that of the United States of America and state of Tennessee may be displayed in or on Tullahoma City Schools buildings, including classrooms, unless it is an official country, state, TCS school, higher education, post secondary institution, or United States military branch flag used solely for educational purposes.

2. Any other flags or other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.), including but not limited to political, cultural, or personal, are prohibited from being displayed in or on Tullahoma City Schools buildings unless it is directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program.

3. The American Flag and State flags shall be displayed in accordance with proper flag etiquette as outlined by the United States Flag Code and applicable state regulations. 

4. The display of flags shall be maintained in good condition and replaced when necessary to ensure proper representation and respect.

5. Any requests for exceptions to this policy must be submitted in writing to the principal/designee for consideration. Organization, club, team sponsors or coaches must submit for exceptions to display any flags connected to their team, club or organization. Within this written request, a clear image of the flag or other display shall be provided, along with clear justification for the requested exception, how it connects directly to club, organization, team or classroom, and the duration for the display.

6. If the principal/designee denies the request, this can be appealed to the Director of Schools/Designee within five business days of the original denial. The Director of Schools/Designee will respond to the appeal request in writing with a decision within five business days. The Director of Schools/Designee's decision will be final. 

7. Any approved request may be revoked by the principal/designee in the event of significant or material disruption within the school day.

The Superintendent, in collaboration with school administrators, shall oversee the implementation of this policy across all Tullahoma City Schools' buildings. School personnel shall ensure compliance with this policy and address any violations promptly and appropriately. Educational initiatives may be undertaken to inform students, staff, and the broader school community about the significance and proper display of the American Flag and Tennessee State flag, as well as the rationale behind this policy, if applicable.

Most complex mathematical equations ever solved
Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
The Navier-Stokes Equations
©Flickr/Raymond Chan
Water flowing through a pipe sounds simple until you try to describe it mathematically. The Navier-Stokes equations govern fluid motion, and they’re so complex that proving whether smooth solutions always exist is worth a million dollars from the Clay Mathematics Institute.

These partial differential equations capture something fundamental about how liquids and gases behave. Weather prediction, airplane design, blood flow through arteries—all depend on solutions to these equations.

The mathematics behind your morning coffee is still partially unsolved.

Story by Joey Esposito • 1mo • 5 min read


An American flag is shown in front of a rainbow. K.C. Alfred / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images
An American flag is shown in front of a rainbow. K.C. Alfred / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images

Claim:

A Tennessee school board voted to enact a policy that banned LGBTQ+ Pride flags and allowed only the United States flag or Tennessee state flag to hang in public schools.

Rating:

Mostly True (About this rating?)

What's True:

The Tullahoma City Schools Board of Education voted to change the district's policy regarding flags and other displays such as "banners, pennants, digital signs, etc." in October 2025. The policy effectively restricted any displays to that of the American flag or Tennessee flag unless "directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program."

 
What's False:

The policy does not call for a ban or removal of Pride flags specifically (although the issue stemmed from complaints about a teacher who displayed a Pride flag in their classroom and was explicitly mentioned as the cause of the discussion within the meeting during which the policy was voted on).

 
A rumor that a school board in Tennessee voted in favor of removing LGBTQ+ Pride flags from public schools swirled online in July 2026. 

People on social media posted about the alleged policy change and claimed the school board voted to allow only flags for the United States and the state of Tennessee. 


View this post on Instagram


In sum, the claim was mostly true. During a Tullahoma City Schools Board of Education meeting on Oct. 21, 2025, the board voted to enact a policy that effectively restricted any displays of flags to the American flag or Tennessee state flag unless "directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program."

The policy does not include language calling for a ban or removal of Pride flags specifically. However, the issue stemmed from complaints about a teacher who displayed a Pride flag in their classroom and was explicitly mentioned as the cause of the discussion during the board meeting in which the policy was voted on.

Expand article logo  Continue reading

During the meeting, which is available to view on the school board's website, the policy passed unanimously. The voting on what is referred to as "Board Policy 4.400" can be seen at the 1:22:00 mark. 

The policy, which was read during the board meeting at the 1:07:00 mark, stated in full: 

In order to regulate flags and other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.) on any/all campuses within Tullahoma City Schools and to ensure a conducive and respectful educational environment, the following guidelines have been established:

1. No flag or other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.) other than that of the United States of America and state of Tennessee may be displayed in or on Tullahoma City Schools buildings, including classrooms, unless it is an official country, state, TCS school, higher education, post secondary institution, or United States military branch flag used solely for educational purposes.

2. Any other flags or other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.), including but not limited to political, cultural, or personal, are prohibited from being displayed in or on Tullahoma City Schools buildings unless it is directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program.

3. The American Flag and State flags shall be displayed in accordance with proper flag etiquette as outlined by the United States Flag Code and applicable state regulations. 

4. The display of flags shall be maintained in good condition and replaced when necessary to ensure proper representation and respect.

5. Any requests for exceptions to this policy must be submitted in writing to the principal/designee for consideration. Organization, club, team sponsors or coaches must submit for exceptions to display any flags connected to their team, club or organization. Within this written request, a clear image of the flag or other display shall be provided, along with clear justification for the requested exception, how it connects directly to club, organization, team or classroom, and the duration for the display.

6. If the principal/designee denies the request, this can be appealed to the Director of Schools/Designee within five business days of the original denial. The Director of Schools/Designee will respond to the appeal request in writing with a decision within five business days. The Director of Schools/Designee's decision will be final. 

7. Any approved request may be revoked by the principal/designee in the event of significant or material disruption within the school day.

The Superintendent, in collaboration with school administrators, shall oversee the implementation of this policy across all Tullahoma City Schools' buildings. School personnel shall ensure compliance with this policy and address any violations promptly and appropriately. Educational initiatives may be undertaken to inform students, staff, and the broader school community about the significance and proper display of the American Flag and Tennessee State flag, as well as the rationale behind this policy, if applicable.

Most complex mathematical equations ever solved
Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
Schrödinger's Equation
©DepositPhotos
Quantum mechanics demanded a new kind of mathematics, and Erwin Schrödinger delivered it in 1926 with an equation that describes how quantum systems evolve over time (though the word “time” itself gets complicated when particles exist in multiple states simultaneously, which is precisely the kind of conceptual knot that makes quantum mechanics feel more like philosophy than physics until you sit down with the actual mathematical machinery). The equation looks deceptively straightforward: iℏ∂ψ/∂t = Ĥψ.

Clean, almost elegant.

But that ψ (psi) represents the wave function—a mathematical object that contains all possible information about a quantum system, and when you start working with systems that have multiple particles, the mathematics explodes into dimensions that have no physical analogue. So the equation that governs everything from electron behavior to the fundamental forces becomes this sprawling, multidimensional beast that requires mathematical techniques most people never encounter: Hilbert spaces, operator theory, functional analysis.

And here’s where it gets strange—the equation is perfectly deterministic, yet it describes a fundamentally probabilistic reality. The mathematics tells you exactly how the wave function evolves, but the wave function itself only gives you probabilities about what you might measure.

The equation works flawlessly; understanding what it means about the nature of reality is another problem entirely.

Most complex mathematical equations ever solved
Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
Einstein's Field Equations
©Flickr/Paul Jones
Gravity isn’t a force—it’s geometry. That insight led Einstein to field equations that describe how mass and energy warp spacetime itself.

The mathematics reads like poetry if you speak tensor calculus: Gμν + Λgμν = 8πTμν.

Each symbol represents layers of complexity that took Einstein years to work through. The left side describes the curvature of spacetime, the right side describes matter and energy.

The equation says they’re equal, which means massive objects literally bend the fabric of reality. The great abyss, GPS satellites, and the expansion of the universe all emerge from solutions to these equations.

The mathematics of curved space predicted phenomena that weren’t observed until decades later.

Most complex mathematical equations ever solved
Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
The Yang-Mills Equations
©Flickr/Brookhaven National Laboratory
Particle physics needed mathematics that could handle symmetries—the idea that certain transformations leave physical laws unchanged. Yang-Mills theory provided that framework in 1954, describing how gauge fields interact with matter particles.

The equations themselves involve non-Abelian gauge theory, fiber bundles, and differential geometry that makes most advanced mathematics look elementary. These aren’t just equations; they’re the mathematical foundation of the Standard Model of particle physics.

Every fundamental interaction except gravity gets described through Yang-Mills theory. The Strong Nuclear Force, the Weak Nuclear Force, electromagnetic interactions—all emerge from solutions to these equations.

6. If the principal/designee denies the request, this can be appealed to the Director of Schools/Designee within five business days of the original denial. The Director of Schools/Designee will respond to the appeal request in writing with a decision within five business days. The Director of Schools/Designee's decision will be final. 

7. Any approved request may be revoked by the principal/designee in the event of significant or material disruption within the school day.

The Superintendent, in collaboration with school administrators, shall oversee the implementation of this policy across all Tullahoma City Schools' buildings. School personnel shall ensure compliance with this policy and address any violations promptly and appropriately. Educational initiatives may be undertaken to inform students, staff, and the broader school community about the significance and proper display of the American Flag and Tennessee State flag, as well as the rationale behind this policy, if applicable.

Most complex mathematical equations ever solved
Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
The Riemann Hypothesis
©Flickr/kmyc89
The distribution of prime numbers follows a pattern that Bernhard Riemann described in 1859 through the Riemann zeta function: ζ(s) = Σ(1/n^s). His hypothesis claims that all non-trivial zeros of this function have real part equal to 1/2.

This conjecture connects number theory to complex analysis in ways that still surprise mathematicians. The hypothesis has been verified for the first 10 trillion zeros, but a general proof remains elusive.

Prime number distribution, cryptography, and dozens of other mathematical results depend on the Riemann Hypothesis being true. It’s mathematics built on faith in a pattern that seems too elegant to be false.

What Tennessee school board's 2025 policy change means for Pride flag displays
Story by Joey Esposito • 1mo • 5 min read


An American flag is shown in front of a rainbow. K.C. Alfred / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images
An American flag is shown in front of a rainbow. K.C. Alfred / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images

Claim:

A Tennessee school board voted to enact a policy that banned LGBTQ+ Pride flags and allowed only the United States flag or Tennessee state flag to hang in public schools.

Rating:

Mostly True (About this rating?)

What's True:

The Tullahoma City Schools Board of Education voted to change the district's policy regarding flags and other displays such as "banners, pennants, digital signs, etc." in October 2025. The policy effectively restricted any displays to that of the American flag or Tennessee flag unless "directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program."

 
What's False:

The policy does not call for a ban or removal of Pride flags specifically (although the issue stemmed from complaints about a teacher who displayed a Pride flag in their classroom and was explicitly mentioned as the cause of the discussion within the meeting during which the policy was voted on).

 
A rumor that a school board in Tennessee voted in favor of removing LGBTQ+ Pride flags from public schools swirled online in July 2026. 

People on social media posted about the alleged policy change and claimed the school board voted to allow only flags for the United States and the state of Tennessee. 


View this post on Instagram


In sum, the claim was mostly true. During a Tullahoma City Schools Board of Education meeting on Oct. 21, 2025, the board voted to enact a policy that effectively restricted any displays of flags to the American flag or Tennessee state flag unless "directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program."

The policy does not include language calling for a ban or removal of Pride flags specifically. However, the issue stemmed from complaints about a teacher who displayed a Pride flag in their classroom and was explicitly mentioned as the cause of the discussion during the board meeting in which the policy was voted on.

Expand article logo  Continue reading

During the meeting, which is available to view on the school board's website, the policy passed unanimously. The voting on what is referred to as "Board Policy 4.400" can be seen at the 1:22:00 mark. 

The policy, which was read during the board meeting at the 1:07:00 mark, stated in full: 

In order to regulate flags and other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.) on any/all campuses within Tullahoma City Schools and to ensure a conducive and respectful educational environment, the following guidelines have been established:

1. No flag or other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.) other than that of the United States of America and state of Tennessee may be displayed in or on Tullahoma City Schools buildings, including classrooms, unless it is an official country, state, TCS school, higher education, post secondary institution, or United States military branch flag used solely for educational purposes.

2. Any other flags or other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.), including but not limited to political, cultural, or personal, are prohibited from being displayed in or on Tullahoma City Schools buildings unless it is directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program.

3. The American Flag and State flags shall be displayed in accordance with proper flag etiquette as outlined by the United States Flag Code and applicable state regulations. 

4. The display of flags shall be maintained in good condition and replaced when necessary to ensure proper representation and respect.

5. Any requests for exceptions to this policy must be submitted in writing to the principal/designee for consideration. Organization, club, team sponsors or coaches must submit for exceptions to display any flags connected to their team, club or organization. Within this written request, a clear image of the flag or other display shall be provided, along with clear justification for the requested exception, how it connects directly to club, organization, team or classroom, and the duration for the display.

6. If the principal/designee denies the request, this can be appealed to the Director of Schools/Designee within five business days of the original denial. The Director of Schools/Designee will respond to the appeal request in writing with a decision within five business days. The Director of Schools/Designee's decision will be final. 

7. Any approved request may be revoked by the principal/designee in the event of significant or material disruption within the school day.

The Superintendent, in collaboration with school administrators, shall oversee the implementation of this policy across all Tullahoma City Schools' buildings. School personnel shall ensure compliance with this policy and address any violations promptly and appropriately. Educational initiatives may be undertaken to inform students, staff, and the broader school community about the significance and proper display of the American Flag and Tennessee State flag, as well as the rationale behind this policy, if applicable.

Most complex mathematical equations ever solved
Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
The Millennium Prize Problems
©Flickr/epsilon_is_afraid_of_zeta
Seven problems define the frontiers of mathematical knowledge (though the Poincaré conjecture has been solved, leaving six that continue to resist solution, each representing a fundamental gap in mathematical understanding that has persisted for decades or centuries). The Clay Mathematics Institute attached million-dollar prizes to each one, which sounds like a publicity stunt until you realize these problems have genuine implications for everything from computer science to theoretical physics.

The P versus NP problem asks whether every problem whose solution can be quickly verified can also be quickly solved—a question that would revolutionize computer science and cryptography if answered definitively. The Hodge conjecture deals with algebraic topology and complex geometry in ways that bridge pure mathematics and theoretical physics.

So these aren’t just abstract mathematical curiosities; they’re questions about the fundamental nature of computation, space, and mathematical truth itself. The prize money is almost irrelevant—solving any of these problems would reshape entire fields of study.

Most complex mathematical equations ever solved
Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture
©Flickr/postechimage
Elliptic curves over rational numbers connect algebraic geometry to number theory in ways that reveal deep patterns about rational solutions to polynomial equations. The BSD conjecture, formulated in the 1960s, relates the rank of an elliptic curve to the behavior of its L-function at a specific point.

The mathematics involves modular forms, complex analysis, and algebraic number theory. Proving this conjecture would unlock new understanding about Diophantine equations—problems about finding integer or rational solutions to polynomial equations.

The conjecture represents one of the most sophisticated attempts to connect different areas of mathematics through a single unifying principle.

Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
The Hodge Conjecture
©DepositPhotos
Algebraic geometry and topology intersect in complex ways when dealing with projective algebraic varieties. The Hodge conjecture proposes that certain topological cycles can be represented as algebraic cycles, bridging the gap between geometric intuition and algebraic rigor.

The mathematics requires knowledge of sheaf theory, cohomology, and complex manifolds. This isn’t just abstract theory—the conjecture addresses fundamental questions about how algebraic and topological properties relate to each other.

Solutions would impact everything from mirror symmetry in theoretical physics to practical applications in algebraic geometry.

What Tennessee school board's 2025 policy change means for Pride flag displays
Story by Joey Esposito • 1mo • 5 min read


An American flag is shown in front of a rainbow. K.C. Alfred / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images
An American flag is shown in front of a rainbow. K.C. Alfred / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images

Claim:

A Tennessee school board voted to enact a policy that banned LGBTQ+ Pride flags and allowed only the United States flag or Tennessee state flag to hang in public schools.

Rating:

Mostly True (About this rating?)

What's True:

The Tullahoma City Schools Board of Education voted to change the district's policy regarding flags and other displays such as "banners, pennants, digital signs, etc." in October 2025. The policy effectively restricted any displays to that of the American flag or Tennessee flag unless "directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program."

 
What's False:

The policy does not call for a ban or removal of Pride flags specifically (although the issue stemmed from complaints about a teacher who displayed a Pride flag in their classroom and was explicitly mentioned as the cause of the discussion within the meeting during which the policy was voted on).

 
A rumor that a school board in Tennessee voted in favor of removing LGBTQ+ Pride flags from public schools swirled online in July 2026. 

People on social media posted about the alleged policy change and claimed the school board voted to allow only flags for the United States and the state of Tennessee. 


View this post on Instagram


In sum, the claim was mostly true. During a Tullahoma City Schools Board of Education meeting on Oct. 21, 2025, the board voted to enact a policy that effectively restricted any displays of flags to the American flag or Tennessee state flag unless "directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program."

The policy does not include language calling for a ban or removal of Pride flags specifically. However, the issue stemmed from complaints about a teacher who displayed a Pride flag in their classroom and was explicitly mentioned as the cause of the discussion during the board meeting in which the policy was voted on.

Expand article logo  Continue reading

During the meeting, which is available to view on the school board's website, the policy passed unanimously. The voting on what is referred to as "Board Policy 4.400" can be seen at the 1:22:00 mark. 

The policy, which was read during the board meeting at the 1:07:00 mark, stated in full: 

In order to regulate flags and other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.) on any/all campuses within Tullahoma City Schools and to ensure a conducive and respectful educational environment, the following guidelines have been established:

1. No flag or other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.) other than that of the United States of America and state of Tennessee may be displayed in or on Tullahoma City Schools buildings, including classrooms, unless it is an official country, state, TCS school, higher education, post secondary institution, or United States military branch flag used solely for educational purposes.

2. Any other flags or other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.), including but not limited to political, cultural, or personal, are prohibited from being displayed in or on Tullahoma City Schools buildings unless it is directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program.

3. The American Flag and State flags shall be displayed in accordance with proper flag etiquette as outlined by the United States Flag Code and applicable state regulations. 

4. The display of flags shall be maintained in good condition and replaced when necessary to ensure proper representation and respect.

5. Any requests for exceptions to this policy must be submitted in writing to the principal/designee for consideration. Organization, club, team sponsors or coaches must submit for exceptions to display any flags connected to their team, club or organization. Within this written request, a clear image of the flag or other display shall be provided, along with clear justification for the requested exception, how it connects directly to club, organization, team or classroom, and the duration for the display.

6. If the principal/designee denies the request, this can be appealed to the Director of Schools/Designee within five business days of the original denial. The Director of Schools/Designee will respond to the appeal request in writing with a decision within five business days. The Director of Schools/Designee's decision will be final. 

7. Any approved request may be revoked by the principal/designee in the event of significant or material disruption within the school day.

The Superintendent, in collaboration with school administrators, shall oversee the implementation of this policy across all Tullahoma City Schools' buildings. School personnel shall ensure compliance with this policy and address any violations promptly and appropriately. Educational initiatives may be undertaken to inform students, staff, and the broader school community about the significance and proper display of the American Flag and Tennessee State flag, as well as the rationale behind this policy, if applicable.

Most complex mathematical equations ever solved
Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
Bessel Functions and Differential Equations
©Unsplash/pawel-czerwinski
Solutions to Bessel’s differential equation appear throughout physics and engineering, describing phenomena from heat conduction to electromagnetic wave propagation. The equation x²y” + xy’ + (x² – n²)y = 0 generates functions that seem abstract but govern real-world behavior.

These functions emerge naturally when solving problems in cylindrical coordinates. Vibrating drumheads, planetary motion, signal processing—all involve Bessel functions as fundamental components.

The mathematics connects pure analysis to physical applications in ways that demonstrate the unexpected unity between abstract theory and practical problems.

Most complex mathematical equations ever solved
Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
The Monster Group
©Flickr/Internet Archive Book Images
Group theory reaches its extreme in the Monster—a finite simple group with approximately 8 × 10^53 elements. The Monster’s existence was predicted before it was constructed, representing the largest of the sporadic groups in the classification of finite simple groups.

Understanding the Monster requires knowledge of character theory, representation theory, and connections to modular functions that surprised mathematicians. The group appears in string theory and algebraic geometry, suggesting deep connections between discrete mathematics and continuous structures.

Its construction and analysis required computational techniques that pushed the boundaries of both theoretical and computational mathematics.

Most complex mathematical equations ever solved
Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
The Atiyah-Singer Index Theorem
©Unsplash/dynamic-wang
Differential geometry meets algebraic topology in the Index Theorem, which relates analytical properties of elliptic differential operators to topological properties of manifolds. The theorem connects the dimension of solution spaces to topological invariants in precise, calculable ways.

This result unified several areas of mathematics that had developed independently. K-theory, differential geometry, and algebraic topology converge in the theorem’s proof and applications.

The mathematics has implications for theoretical physics, particularly in understanding anomalies in quantum field theory and the geometric foundations of gauge theories.

Any other flags or other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.), including but not limited to political, cultural, or personal, are prohibited from being displayed in or on Tullahoma City Schools buildings unless it is directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program.

3. The American Flag and State flags shall be displayed in accordance with proper flag etiquette as outlined by the United States Flag Code and applicable state regulations. 

4. The display of flags shall be maintained in good condition and replaced when necessary to ensure proper representation and respect.

5. Any requests for exceptions to this policy must be submitted in writing to the principal/designee for consideration. Organization, club, team sponsors or coaches must submit for exceptions to display any flags connected to their team, club or organization. Within this written request, a clear image of the flag or other display shall be provided, along with clear justification for the requested exception, how it connects directly to club, organization, team or classroom, and the duration for the display.

6. If the principal/designee denies the request, this can be appealed to the Director of Schools/Designee within five business days of the original denial. The Director of Schools/Designee will respond to the appeal request in writing with a decision within five business days. The Director of Schools/Designee's decision will be final. 

7. Any approved request may be revoked by the principal/designee in the event of significant or material disruption within the school day.

The Superintendent, in collaboration with school administrators, shall oversee the implementation of this policy across all Tullahoma City Schools' buildings. School personnel shall ensure compliance with this policy and address any violations promptly and appropriately. Educational initiatives may be undertaken to inform students, staff, and the broader school community about the significance and proper display of the American Flag and Tennessee State flag, as well as the rationale behind this policy, if applicable.

Most complex mathematical equations ever solved
Story by Adam Garcia • 3mo
The Langlands Program
©DepositPhotos
Number theory and representation theory connect through a vast network of conjectures known as the Langlands Program. These conjectures propose deep relationships between Galois groups, automorphic forms, and L-functions that would unify large areas of mathematics.

The program involves harmonic analysis, algebraic number theory, and representation theory of p-adic groups. Proving the Langlands conjectures would establish connections between number theory and geometry that many consider the most ambitious unification project in modern mathematics.

Parts of the program have been proven, but the full scope remains an open challenge.

What Tennessee school board's 2025 policy change means for Pride flag displays
Story by Joey Esposito • 1mo • 5 min read


An American flag is shown in front of a rainbow. K.C. Alfred / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images
An American flag is shown in front of a rainbow. K.C. Alfred / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images

Claim:

A Tennessee school board voted to enact a policy that banned LGBTQ+ Pride flags and allowed only the United States flag or Tennessee state flag to hang in public schools.

Rating:

Mostly True (About this rating?)

What's True:

The Tullahoma City Schools Board of Education voted to change the district's policy regarding flags and other displays such as "banners, pennants, digital signs, etc." in October 2025. The policy effectively restricted any displays to that of the American flag or Tennessee flag unless "directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program."

 
What's False:

The policy does not call for a ban or removal of Pride flags specifically (although the issue stemmed from complaints about a teacher who displayed a Pride flag in their classroom and was explicitly mentioned as the cause of the discussion within the meeting during which the policy was voted on).

 
A rumor that a school board in Tennessee voted in favor of removing LGBTQ+ Pride flags from public schools swirled online in July 2026. 

People on social media posted about the alleged policy change and claimed the school board voted to allow only flags for the United States and the state of Tennessee. 


View this post on Instagram


In sum, the claim was mostly true. During a Tullahoma City Schools Board of Education meeting on Oct. 21, 2025, the board voted to enact a policy that effectively restricted any displays of flags to the American flag or Tennessee state flag unless "directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program."

The policy does not include language calling for a ban or removal of Pride flags specifically. However, the issue stemmed from complaints about a teacher who displayed a Pride flag in their classroom and was explicitly mentioned as the cause of the discussion during the board meeting in which the policy was voted on.

Expand article logo  Continue reading

During the meeting, which is available to view on the school board's website, the policy passed unanimously. The voting on what is referred to as "Board Policy 4.400" can be seen at the 1:22:00 mark. 

The policy, which was read during the board meeting at the 1:07:00 mark, stated in full: 

In order to regulate flags and other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.) on any/all campuses within Tullahoma City Schools and to ensure a conducive and respectful educational environment, the following guidelines have been established:

1. No flag or other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.) other than that of the United States of America and state of Tennessee may be displayed in or on Tullahoma City Schools buildings, including classrooms, unless it is an official country, state, TCS school, higher education, post secondary institution, or United States military branch flag used solely for educational purposes.

2. Any other flags or other displays (ex., banners, pennants, digital signs, etc.), including but not limited to political, cultural, or personal, are prohibited from being displayed in or on Tullahoma City Schools buildings unless it is directly related to the curriculum or other school-sanctioned event or program.

3. The American Flag and State flags shall be displayed in accordance with proper flag etiquette as outlined by the United States Flag Code and applicable state regulations. 

4. The display of flags shall be maintained in good condition and replaced when necessary to ensure proper representation and respect.

5. Any requests for exceptions to this policy must be submitted in writing to the principal/designee for consideration. Organization, club, team sponsors or coaches must submit for exceptions to display any flags connected to their team, club or organization. Within this written request, a clear image of the flag or other display shall be provided, along with clear justification for the requested exception, how it connects directly to club, organization, team or classroom, and the duration for the display.

6. If the principal/designee denies the request, this can be appealed to the Director of Schools/Designee within five business days of the original denial. The Director of Schools/Designee will respond to the appeal request in writing with a decision within five business days. The Director of Schools/Designee's decision will be final. 

7. Any approved request may be revoked by the principal/designee in the event of significant or material disruption within the school day.

The Superintendent, in collaboration with school administrators, shall oversee the implementation of this policy across all Tullahoma City Schools' buildings. School personnel shall ensure compliance with this policy and address any violations promptly and appropriately. Educational initiatives may be undertaken to inform students, staff, and the broader school community about the significance and proper display of the American Flag and Tennessee State flag, as well as the rationale behind this policy, if applicable.

Is time travel possible? What Albert Einstein's theory of relativity tells us
Story by Disita Sikdar • 1mo
Einstein changed how we understand time and space
©Central Press/Getty Images and StoneCold Coffee Photography/Getty Images/iStockphoto
The theory of relativity, proposed by Albert Einstein in two parts in 1905 and 1915, fundamentally changed our understanding of the universe. Einstein demonstrated that time and space can stretch or compress depending on speed and gravity, meaning that time does not pass at the same rate everywhere. A second on the surface of Earth is slightly different from a second experienced by a satellite orbiting the planet. Rather than massive objects like stars and planets simply pushing down on space, their mass warps the fabric of spacetime itself, creating the effect we feel as gravity. Through his theories, Einstein was describing real physical changes, not just illusions, and these concepts became the scientific foundation for exploring whether traveling through time could ever be possible.

This is an image of German-born American physicist Albert Einstein (1879 - 1955) (L) and a stock photo representing warped time (R).

Does law make lending someone your car a federal offense starting in November?
Story by Laerke Christensen • 1mo • 4 min read


A white person wearing a blue sweater drops a set of car keys into the hand of a white person wearing a grey top. Getty Images, accessed via Canva
A white person wearing a blue sweater drops a set of car keys into the hand of a white person wearing a grey top. Getty Images, accessed via Canva

Claim:

From Nov. 22, lending your vehicle to a person who is not the registered owner will be a federal offense resulting in a $1000 fine.

Rating:

False (About this rating?)

In July 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that, starting Nov. 22, lending a vehicle to anyone other than the registered owner would be a federal offense resulting in a $1,000 fine.

For example, one Facebook page shared the claim on July 23, 2026. The page's post featured a video with a robotic voice that said: 

Starting November 22, lending your vehicle to anyone will officially be considered a federal offense. The new regulation goes into effect without exceptions and only the person registered on the vehicle's documentation will be legally allowed to drive it. The penalty is immediate — a $1,000 fine on the spot with no warnings, no grace period and no excuses, not even family emergencies. Authorities have already activated a nationwide verification system. Patrol units can now scan a license plate and instantly confirm whether the driver matches the registered owner. If they don't, the vehicle will be seized and the driver will be fined. Officials claim the measure is meant to bring more order and control to the roads but millions of people are already calling it excessive, restrictive and disruptive to everyday life. Beginning November 22nd, something as simple as letting your child, a friend or even a neighbor borrow your car will automatically qualify as a serious violation. There will be no tolerance, no exceptions, no quick appeals. Every entry will be logged digitally and any mismatch will be punished immediately. This new policy is about to impact millions of people quietly and abruptly. Share this message before more people get caught off guard.

Related Facebook post

Shared from Facebook

The claim also circulated elsewhere on Facebook (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.

Riley Gaines called WNBA fans in Minneapolis a 'bunch of disgruntled lesbians'
Story by Nur Ibrahim • 2d • 3 min read


Oliver Contreras, accessed via Getty Images.
Oliver Contreras, accessed via Getty Images.

Claim:

Former NCAA swimmer Riley Gaines called WNBA fans in Minneapolis a “bunch of disgruntled lesbians.”

Rating:

Correct Attribution (About this rating?)

In September 2026, a claim circulated online that former NCAA swimmer Riley Gaines, who is now a conservative pundit, called Women's National Basketball Association fans in Minneapolis "a bunch of disgruntled lesbians." 

The purported quote spread on X (archived), Facebook and Instagram (archived), along with clips of Gaines. She reportedly said:

I went to the WNBA game in Minneapolis… it was a bunch of disgruntled lesbians. It felt like the entire arena was booing Sophie Cunningham.

Gaines did indeed make the above remarks on Fox News' "The Big Weekend Show" on Sept. 5. As such, we've rated this claim as a correct attribution. 

Gaines was responding to a question from host Tomi Lahren, who asked why the WNBA wouldn't define a "woman." We have reproduced the exchange below (emphasis ours):

Story by Stars Insider • 5mo
Clock adjustment
©Shutterstock
The clocks in the sky click faster than the clocks on Earth. Because of this, the ones in the sky must be constantly readjusted to ensure accuracy. If not, your map app could be inaccurate by about six miles (10 km) per day!

Story by Stars Insider • 5mo
Closed-circle loop theory
©Shutterstock
Without evidence for the existence of a closed-circle loop, there is no way to recreate it. A philosopher at Chapman University in California, Emily Adlam, says, "Even if we had much greater technological powers than we currently do, it seems unlikely that we would be able to create closed time-like curves on purpose."

The purported quote spread on X (archived), Facebook and Instagram (archived), along with clips of Gaines. She reportedly said:

I went to the WNBA game in Minneapolis… it was a bunch of disgruntled lesbians. It felt like the entire arena was booing Sophie Cunningham.

Gaines did indeed make the above remarks on Fox News' "The Big Weekend Show" on Sept. 5. As such, we've rated this claim as a correct attribution.

It felt like virtually everyone in that arena, first of all, you audibly heard it, anytime Sophie was subbed in, stepped on the court, touched the ball, threw up a shot, her name was announced on the loudspeakers … you heard the entire arena boo. It felt like they had been advised to only put people on the jumbotron who were draped in their trans flag … And the general public knows that is not indicative of real life.

The full episode has been archived and the exchange takes place after 2:38 p.m. 

Gaines was referring to Sophie Cunningham, a WNBA player with the Indiana Fever, who has expressed opposition to transgender players' participation in women's sports. Gaines and Cunningham have also been photographed (archived) together.

In September 2026, a claim circulated online that former NCAA swimmer Riley Gaines, who is now a conservative pundit, called Women's National Basketball Association fans in Minneapolis "a bunch of disgruntled lesbians." 

The purported quote spread on X (archived), Facebook and Instagram (archived), along with clips of Gaines. She reportedly said:

I went to the WNBA game in Minneapolis… it was a bunch of disgruntled lesbians. It felt like the entire arena was booing Sophie Cunningham.

Gaines did indeed make the above remarks on Fox News' "The Big Weekend Show" on Sept. 5. As such, we've rated this claim as a correct attribution. 

Gaines was responding to a question from host Tomi Lahren, who asked why the WNBA wouldn't define a "woman." We have reproduced the exchange below (emphasis ours):

Lahren: …but what I find here so interesting is the WNBA with a "W" in their name, they won't define a woman. And I can't figure out if it's because they have players that are currently playing that wouldn't fit that definition … or is it because they don't want to anger what they feel is a large part of their fanbase that is LGBTQ? Or is it a little bit of both? 

Gaines: I'm sure it's a little bit of both. I can tell you. I went to the WNBA game in Minneapolis. Which you can expect … what the fanbase as it pertains to the WNBA in that city looks like. And it was a bunch of, like, disgruntled lesbians. And I think that the WNBA as a league, organizationally they recognize that. It felt like virtually everyone in that arena, first of all, you audibly heard it, anytime Sophie was subbed in, stepped on the court, touched the ball, threw up a shot, her name was announced on the loudspeakers … you heard the entire arena boo. It felt like they had been advised to only put people on the jumbotron who were draped in their trans flag … And the general public knows that is not indicative of real life. 

Expand article logo  Continue reading

The full episode has been archived and the exchange takes place after 2:38 p.m. 

Gaines was referring to Sophie Cunningham, a WNBA player with the Indiana Fever, who has expressed opposition to transgender players' participation in women's sports. Gaines and Cunningham have also been photographed (archived) together.

What physics says about time travel
Story by Stars Insider • 5mo
Retrocausality
©Shutterstock
In response, some physicists have come up with an alternative way to interpret the experiments. Some propose that when something looks instantaneous, it has actually traveled to the future and back again. This introduces retrocausality, i.e. events that take place in the future having an effect on the past.

Former NCAA swimmer Riley Gaines called WNBA fans in Minneapolis a “bunch of disgruntled lesbians.”

Rating:

Correct Attribution (About this rating?)

In September 2026, a claim circulated online that former NCAA swimmer Riley Gaines, who is now a conservative pundit, called Women's National Basketball Association fans in Minneapolis "a bunch of disgruntled lesbians." 

The purported quote spread on X (archived), Facebook and Instagram (archived), along with clips of Gaines. She reportedly said:

I went to the WNBA game in Minneapolis… it was a bunch of disgruntled lesbians. It felt like the entire arena was booing Sophie Cunningham.

Gaines did indeed make the above remarks on Fox News' "The Big Weekend Show" on Sept. 5. As such, we've rated this claim as a correct attribution. 

Gaines was responding to a question from host Tomi Lahren, who asked why the WNBA wouldn't define a "woman." We have reproduced the exchange below (emphasis ours):

Lahren: …but what I find here so interesting is the WNBA with a "W" in their name, they won't define a woman. And I can't figure out if it's because they have players that are currently playing that wouldn't fit that definition … or is it because they don't want to anger what they feel is a large part of their fanbase that is LGBTQ? Or is it a little bit of both? 

Gaines: I'm sure it's a little bit of both. I can tell you. I went to the WNBA game in Minneapolis. Which you can expect … what the fanbase as it pertains to the WNBA in that city looks like. And it was a bunch of, like, disgruntled lesbians. And I think that the WNBA as a league, organizationally they recognize that. It felt like virtually everyone in that arena, first of all, you audibly heard it, anytime Sophie was subbed in, stepped on the court, touched the ball, threw up a shot, her name was announced on the loudspeakers … you heard the entire arena boo. It felt like they had been advised to only put people on the jumbotron who were draped in their trans flag … And the general public knows that is not indicative of real life.

The full episode has been archived and the exchange takes place after 2:38 p.m. 

Gaines was referring to Sophie Cunningham, a WNBA player with the Indiana Fever, who has expressed opposition to transgender players' participation in women's sports. Gaines and Cunningham have also been photographed (archived) together.

For now, time travel remains out of reach—just like the more mysterious workings of the universe.

Riley Gaines called WNBA fans in Minneapolis a 'bunch of disgruntled lesbians'
Story by Nur Ibrahim • 2d • 3 min read


Oliver Contreras, accessed via Getty Images.
Oliver Contreras, accessed via Getty Images.

Former NCAA swimmer Riley Gaines called WNBA fans in Minneapolis a “bunch of disgruntled lesbians.”

Popular space facts that are totally wrong
Story by Alexander Clark • 9mo • 6 min read


Popular space facts that are totally wrong
Popular space facts that are totally wrong
I grew up loving space documentaries, so I was genuinely annoyed when I realized how many “facts” I’d absorbed were just slick-sounding myths. The universe is already strange enough on its own; we don’t need bad science muddying the picture. Here, I’m unpacking some of the most common space misconceptions I still hear all the time—and what actually holds up when you look at the physics instead of the hype.

Join Millions Playing
Join Millions Playing
top5onlinegames.com
top5onlinegames.com
·
Sponsored
call to action icon
The Moon’s “dark side” isn’t actually dark
I still hear people talk about the “dark side of the Moon” as if half of our satellite lives in permanent night, which makes for great song lyrics but terrible astronomy. The far side of the Moon—the hemisphere we never see from Earth—gets just as much sunlight as the near side; it’s only “dark” in the sense that it’s unknown to us. The Moon is tidally locked, so the same face always points toward Earth, but as it orbits, day and night sweep across both hemispheres in a slow two-week cycle.

What really changes is our vantage point, not the Sun’s light. When the near side is lit up as a full Moon, the far side is experiencing lunar night; two weeks later, the far side is in full daylight while we see a new Moon. Visual explainers that walk through this geometry make it clear that “dark side” is a misnomer and that the far side has craters, mountains, and even landing sites bathed in sunlight, just like the hemisphere we know so well, as shown in detailed orbital animations in videos such as lunar phase breakdowns.

You would not instantly freeze in the vacuum of space
The idea that an unprotected astronaut would flash-freeze the moment they stepped into space is one of those movie tropes that refuses to die. In reality, space is cold in the sense that it doesn’t provide heat, but it’s also almost empty, which means there’s nothing to conduct that heat away from your body quickly. You’d have a lot of other problems first—like lack of oxygen and pressure—long before you turned into a human icicle.

Without a suit, the air in your lungs would rush out, you’d lose consciousness in seconds, and exposed tissues would swell because there’s no external pressure, but your core temperature would drop more slowly as you radiated heat away. Demonstrations that compare conduction, convection, and radiation show why heat loss in a vacuum is surprisingly slow, and why spacecraft rely on radiators and careful thermal control rather than just “letting space cool things down,” a point that’s often emphasized in physics explainers like vacuum exposure simulations.

Tirzepatide: The GLP1 That Crushes It
Direct Meds GLP-1
Direct Meds GLP-1

call to action icon
Black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners
The drama only ramps up when you get close enough that the black hole’s gravity changes rapidly over short distances, stretching and heating matter into bright, swirling disks instead of quietly “vacuuming” it. Astrophysicists often point out that stars can orbit black holes stably for millions of years, and that the chaotic accretion we see in images is a local effect near the event horizon, not a galaxy-wide drain, a nuance that comes up frequently in discussions of weird but real black hole behavior.

Asteroid belts are mostly empty space
If your mental image of the asteroid belt comes from sci‑fi, you probably picture starships weaving through dense clouds of tumbling rocks. The reality is almost disappointingly sparse. The main belt between Mars and Jupiter contains countless objects, but they’re spread over such a huge volume that the average distance between sizable asteroids is hundreds of thousands of kilometers. A spacecraft could fly through without ever needing to dodge anything.

Learn Piano As An Adult Easily - Playing Piano Was Never Easier - Learn Piano Easily At Any Age
Learn Piano As An Adult Easily - Playing Piano Was Never Easier - Learn Piano Easily At Any Age

call to action icon
That emptiness is exactly why missions like NASA’s probes can thread the belt with minimal risk, relying on careful tracking rather than arcade‑style reflexes. Visualizations that scale the belt correctly show more empty black than rock, and mission briefings often stress that the biggest hazard is radiation and long-duration travel, not collisions with swarms of boulders, a point that’s reinforced in orbital dynamics breakdowns like asteroid belt simulations.

Space is not completely silent
When scientists “record” black holes or nebulae, they’re often measuring pressure waves or electromagnetic signals and converting them into audible frequencies, a process called sonification. That doesn’t mean a human floating nearby would hear a Hollywood-style roar, but it does mean the cosmos is full of vibrations that can be translated into sound. Some outreach projects have turned real data into eerie audio tracks, illustrating how ripples in hot gas around galaxy clusters can be mapped to tones, as in several popular space sonification clips that circulate on social platforms.

“Weightlessness” in orbit doesn’t mean zero gravity
This is the same physics that governs a roller coaster’s brief moments of weightlessness, just stretched out over an entire orbit. Educational videos often show how you can recreate the effect with a drop tower or parabolic flight, where instruments and people float for seconds at a time, illustrating that “zero‑g” is really “microgravity” caused by free fall, not an absence of gravitational pull, a distinction that’s central to many orbital mechanics explainers.

The Great Wall of China is not uniquely visible from space
What really matters for visibility is contrast and size, not cultural significance. Bright runways, sprawling suburbs, and even long bridges can stand out far more than the Wall. Fact‑checking pieces on everyday myths have repeatedly debunked the idea that the Great Wall is uniquely visible, grouping it alongside other persistent misconceptions about human structures and the view from orbit, as detailed in breakdowns of popular “facts” that don’t hold up.

Stars do not twinkle in space the way they do from Earth
This is one reason space telescopes like Hubble can capture such sharp images: they’re looking at stars without the atmospheric shimmer that blurs ground-based views. Side‑by‑side comparisons of ground and orbital observations show how much clarity you gain once you’re above the air, and many observing guides emphasize that the “twinkle” is a local effect, not an intrinsic property of stars themselves, a point that’s often highlighted in atmospheric distortion demonstrations.

The Sun is not a “yellow” star up close
When you remove the atmosphere from the equation—as satellites and space probes effectively do—the Sun appears as a bright white star. Spectral measurements confirm that its output peaks in the visible range and spans colors our eyes blend into white, which is why daylight on a clear day looks white even if the Sun itself seems yellowish. Many solar physics videos walk through this spectrum and show space-based imagery where the Sun’s true appearance is closer to white, a nuance that’s easy to see in spaceborne solar observations.

Not all “shooting stars” are big chunks of rock
Only a small fraction of incoming material is large enough to survive the journey and land as meteorites, and those are the rare specimens that end up in museum cases or private collections. Observing guides and meteor shower explainers repeatedly stress how small most of these particles are, and how the spectacle comes from speed and energy, not size, a point that’s illustrated vividly in high‑speed footage and breakdowns like meteor entry visualizations.

Space myths stick because the real universe is hard to picture
When I look back at the misconceptions I once believed, a pattern jumps out: almost all of them come from trying to force the universe into everyday intuition. We picture black holes as drains because that’s how water behaves, assume space is freezing because winter feels cold, and imagine asteroid belts as crowded because that’s what makes a good movie chase scene. Our brains lean on familiar analogies, even when the physics is nothing like what we experience on Earth.

The good news is that the real story is far more interesting than the myths. Once you start digging into how gravity actually works, how light travels, and how thin our atmosphere really is compared with the scale of space, the universe stops being a backdrop for clichés and becomes a place where your intuition has to stretch. That’s why I keep going back to clear, visual explanations—from orbital animations to hands‑on demos like microgravity experiments—because the more accurately we picture space, the more awe it inspires without needing any exaggeration at all.

Does Quaker instant strawberries and cream oatmeal contain beaver butt secretions?
Story by Jordan Liles • 1mo • 5 min read


A photo shows boxes of Quaker oatmeal on a store shelf, specifically the instant variety of strawberries and cream. Jordan Liles via Snopes.com
A photo shows boxes of Quaker oatmeal on a store shelf, specifically the instant variety of strawberries and cream. Jordan Liles via Snopes.com

A long-standing online rumor claims the "natural flavor" ingredient listed on boxes of Quaker Oats' instant strawberries and cream oatmeal secretly contains castoreum, an oily substance derived from an area near a beaver's anal glands.
A spokesperson for PepsiCo, the company that owns Quaker, denied the rumor, saying, "The claim is inaccurate. The flavoring used in Quaker Instant Oatmeal Strawberries & Cream does not contain castoreum."
Snopes was not able to independently verify this claim and therefore did not apply a fact-check rating.
A 1977 Federal Register document shows castoreum receiving a "Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS)" classification in the Code of Federal Regulations. A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, speaking generally about food products, said that classification was specifically "for use as a natural flavoring agent," adding the substance may appear on ingredients labels "simply as 'natural flavoring.'" 
For years, people have shared videos about the Quaker Oats Co.'s instant strawberries and cream oatmeal, alleging the product box's "natural flavor" ingredient secretly contains castoreum — an oily substance with a vanillalike scent derived from an area near a beaver's anal glands.

In one example, a YouTube video (archived) from May 2026 combined clips from other users' videos, including from author and creator Jabez el Israel (@jabez_invests), who has recorded multiple clips promoting the rumor. The YouTube video also showed part of a 2013 clip from author Vani Hari, known online under the name Food Babe.


The rumor has also appeared on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Reddit (archived), TikTok (archived) and X (archived).

Expand article logo  Continue reading

In short, Snopes was not able to independently verify this rumor. For that reason, we did not apply a fact-check rating to this story.

We emailed PepsiCo, Quaker's parent company, to ask whether PepsiCo uses castoreum in Quaker strawberries and cream instant oatmeal or any other products, as well as to request a list of ingredients that make up the "natural flavor" displayed on the box.
